1. A woman in her 30s presented with multiple discrete and clustered blue papules on her face and extremities. | 2. The pain associated with these papules worsened as the day progressed, and she could not tolerate elastic compression due to excessive pain on compression. | 4. Her medical and family histories were unremarkable. | 5. Physical examination revealed multiple discrete and agminated blue papules on the face, arms, hands, and thighs with a cobblestoned appearance (Figure 1). | 6. On palpation, the papules were exquisitely tender and partially compressible. | 8. Clinically, multiple discrete and agminated blue papules are apparent, nodular, blue cutaneous lesions cobblestone-like in appearance, on the thigh (A) and hand and thigh (B).

1. A 60-year-old man with a history of IgA kappa multiple myeloma was referred to our department. | 2. He had been diagnosed with multiple myeloma 2 years earlier after discovery of osteolytic bone lesions of the skull and the findings of a bone marrow biopsy. | 3. The patient had been treated with bortezomib and dexamethasone followed by autologous blood progenitor cell transplantation, which resulted in complete response. | 4. At the time of the consultation, he was free of disease.The patient was referred for evaluation of an indolent, erythematous papule on his glans penis of 2 weeks’ duration. | 5. He denied sexual risk behavior and reported no recent changes in medication. | 6. Careful physical examination revealed a shiny, tense, erythematous, hemispherical papule measuring 5 mm in diameter located on the lateral aspect of the glans (Figure 1A). | 7. There were no other skin lesions. | 8. The lymph nodes were not palpable, and there was no organomegaly.

Computed tomography (CT) showed a right-sided grade IV renal injury involving his known renal cyst with active arterial extravasation (Figure, A). | 3. 1. The patient is a 48-year-old man with a history of a rectal adenocarcinoma (cT3N2bM0) diagnosed 9 years prior. | 2. Following neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, low anterior resection, and 6 cycles of adjuvant FOLFOX therapy (fluorouracil, leucovorin, and oxaliplatin), he had developed a lung metastasis (KRAS wild type) 1 year later. | 3. He subsequently developed multiple lung metastases treated with palliative local interventions (lobectomy, radiofrequency ablation) and 4 lines of chemotherapy. | 4. Owing to symptomatic lung disease, he was enrolled in a clinical trial (NCT03502733) following informed consent and achieved a confirmed partial response. | 5. After 9 months, contrast computed tomography restaging scans noted a new, 1-cm posterior subglottic lesion of unclear origin (Figure, A). | 6. He had no shortness of breath or noisy breathing, dysphagia, voice change, or hemoptysis. | 7. A partial response was maintained without evidence of progression of lung disease.A, An axial computed tomographic image reveals a new posterior subglottic lesion (pink arrowhead) of unclear etiology. | 10. The differential diagnosis based on imaging included a mass vs inspissated mucus. | 11. Examination using distal-chip flexible laryngoscopy revealed a 1-cm, broad-based, exophytic mass along the posterior wall of the subglottis with prominent vasculature. | 12. No other anatomic abnormalities in the upper aerodigestive tract or cervical lymphadenopathy were noted. | 13. The decision was made to proceed to the operating room for definitive endoscopic biopsy under general anesthesia (Figure, B). | 14. Examination revealed a subglottic mass that did not extend inferiorly beyond the caudal aspect of the cricoid cartilage. | 15. The mass was debulked and sent to pathology for analysis, including hematoxylin-eosin and immunohistochemical staining (Figure, C).

He denied vision changes, light sensitivity, or drainage from the eye. | 4. He denied previous similar episodes of eyelid swelling or recurrent chalazia. | 5. He had no relevant medical history and his family history was negative for malignancy. | 6. The eyelid demonstrated mild boggy edema; however, there were no associated nodules, vesicles, or plaques on the surrounding skin or face. | 8. There was mild madarosis in the area of ulceration. | 9. There was also a tender and enlarged preauricular lymph node on the ipsilateral side. | 10. The remainder of the clinical examination was unremarkable, including visual acuity, intraocular pressure, slitlamp biomicroscopy, and dilated fundus examination. | 12. A, External photograph of the left eye demonstrating central upper eyelid margin ulceration with sparse lashes and surrounding edema. | 13. B, Incisional biopsy reveals a necrotic epithelium with multinucleated keratinocytes and cytoplasmic inclusions (hematoxylin-eosin, ×200).

1. A man in his 70s presented to the clinic with a split in the right fifth fingernail for the past 10 years. | 2. He reported paroxysmal, intermittent pain that was exacerbated by cold weather. | 3. He fractured the digit more than 30 years earlier. | 4. Physical examination revealed distal nail plate splitting with accompanying longitudinal erythronychia (Figure, A) and tenderness on palpation of the nail unit. | 5. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a nail matrix lesion (Figure, B), which was excised using a transungual approach with partial nail avulsion. | 6. The specimen was analyzed by histopathology (Figure, C and D).

1. A 24-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-day history of a red, itchy rash on his buttocks and legs. | 2. Four days ago, he returned from a cruise to the Caribbean, during which he swam in the ship’s pool and used the hot tub.

No other abnormalities were found on ophthalmoscopic examination. | 10. 1. A 57-year-old woman with a medical history of recurrent biliary colic was admitted with symptoms consistent with mild gallstone pancreatitis. | 2. Routine laboratory test results showed total bilirubin of 4.74 mg/dL (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 17.104) and amylase of 1.041 U/L (to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167). | 3. An abdominal ultrasonography scan demonstrated gallstones and a mildly dilated common bile duct (CBD). | 4. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen confirmed these results and revealed cholelithiasis. | 5. The patient consequently underwent urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy with intraoperative cholangiography (Figure, A). | 6. Intraoperative cholangiography revealed an unusual anatomical variant and subsequent transcystic choledochoscopy was performed, which demonstrated a double lumen at the distal CBD (Figure, B). | 7. Multiple gallstones were found within a dilated region of cystic duct.

He also reported recent-onset headache while reading. | 4. The nodules were firm, mobile, and nontender on palpation. | 6. Local temperature was normal. | 7. There was proptosis of the right eye with mild restriction of extraocular movements on lateral gaze. | 10. Respiratory system examination revealed occasional polyphonic wheeze. | 11. Chest radiography imaging showed nodular opacities in right upper zone and bronchiectasis. | 15. C, High-power view showing epithelioid cell granulomas and fungal profiles within giant cells (arrowheads). | 16. 1. A man in his early 30s presented with 4 days of acute, monocular, painless vision loss. | 2. His visual acuity was 20/200 OD and 20/20 OS. | 3. There was no afferent pupillary defect, his color vision was intact bilaterally, and his intraocular pressures were normal. | 4. No anterior chamber or vitreal inflammation was present. | 5. Ophthalmoscopic examination of the right macula revealed a 2–disc diameter area of heterogeneous yellow retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) discoloration with overlying neurosensory retinal detachment and several small retinal hemorrhages (Figure 1A). | 6. The optic disc and retinal vessels were unremarkable, and ophthalmoscopic examination of the left eye revealed no abnormalities.A, Fundus photography of the right eye shows retinal pigment epithelial discoloration and retinal hemorrhages. | 7. B, Optical coherence tomography demonstrates neurosensory retinal detachment overlying irregular retinal pigment epithelium and thickened choroid.The patient denied recent corticosteroid use, joint pain, weight loss, myalgias, or cardiovascular, neurologic, or gastrointestinal symptoms. | 8. He had fevers and mild upper respiratory tract symptoms 2 weeks before his presentation, closely followed by a rash on his hands and thighs. | 9. A young family member had similar symptoms.Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) revealed a fovea-involving neurosensory retinal detachment, outer photoreceptor thickening, and an intact external limiting membrane overlying a zone of mildly thickened, irregular RPE. | 10. The submacular choroid was relatively thick bilaterally on enhanced depth imaging OCT (Figure 1B). | 11. Combined fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography demonstrated mottled early hyperfluorescence with late staining and minimal pooling. | 12. There was no leakage from the retinal vessels or optic discs bilaterally, and uninvolved areas of RPE and choroidal vasculature were unremarkable. | 13. A test for rapid plasma reagin was negative.Observe; follow up in 4 to 6 weeks with SD-OCTTreat with intravitreal antivascular endothelial growth factor injection

1. A woman in her 50s presented to a tertiary dermatology referral center with scaly erythematous patches and plaques covering 10% of her total body surface area without clinically appreciable lymphadenopathy. | 2. An initial deltoid muscle biopsy did not show evidence of myopathy.

1. A 40-year-old man of Scandinavian descent presented with enlarging, nonpainful upper extremity nodules developing over the preceding 9 months (Figure, A). | 4. Also, he developed a pathological fracture of his right foot (Figure, B). | 8. Medications included glipizide, metformin, and levothyroxine.A, Nodules are 4 to 6 cm in diameter on the right upper extremity. | 12. 1. A 64-year-old woman with borderline resectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma and a history of hormone receptor–positive left-sided breast cancer (treated with lumpectomy and radiation in 2014) was transferred to our hospital for management of a displaced percutaneous hepatobiliary drain. | 2. She was diagnosed as having pancreatic adenocarcinoma in September 2019 after developing right upper quadrant pain and jaundice, which prompted imaging and a subsequent endoscopic biopsy of a pancreatic head mass. | 4. Her posttreatment course was complicated by elevated levels of transaminases, significant fatigue, and an infusion port thrombosis. | 5. Her infusion port (right sided) was subsequently removed, and she was given 1.5 mg/kg of enoxaparin daily for anticoagulation. | 7. 1. A woman in her mid-50s presented to the clinic with a 6-month history of progressive swelling and pain on the right side of her neck. | 2. She had increasing fatigue during the last 6 months, as well as worsening anxiety. | 4. On physical examination, the neck was supple, with no palpable masses or lymphadenopathy, and had a well-healed transverse neck incision. | 5. T1-weighted image (A) and T2-weighted image (B) revealing a round, partially enhancing, cystic mass near the tail of the parotid gland (white and red arrowheads).

1. A woman in her 20s was referred for evaluation of a 4-year history of recurrent pustular eruptions on her face, which initially presented while she was vacationing in Florida. | 2. The eruptions occurred intermittently, appearing as erythematous papules with prominent pustules, and were exacerbated by sunlight. | 4. On average, her lesions would resolve in 3 to 4 days with only mild background erythema by 5 to 7 days. | 5. Even mild sun exposure would induce the eruption, leading to frequent recurrences in summer months but long periods of remission in the fall through spring. | 6. Trials with various broad-spectrum sunscreens in combination with topical and oral antibiotics and topical ivermectin did not prevent flares or mitigate severity of eruptions when they occurred. | 7. She denied joint pain, fever, fatigue, changes in urine color, use of other topical or systemic medications, or presence of rashes elsewhere. | 8. She was otherwise healthy without other medical history. | 9. On physical examination, she was well appearing with numerous 1- to 2-mm monomorphous pustules over background erythema on the medial cheeks, chin, and nose (Figure, A). | 10. 1. A woman in her 60s presented 1 week after undergoing cataract surgery in the right eye complaining of persistent blurry vision. | 2. Her ocular history was notable for a previous uncomplicated cataract surgery in the left eye that had a good visual outcome. | 3. On postoperative day 1, her visual acuity was 20/60 OD, attributed to mild corneal edema, with an intraocular pressure of 18 mm Hg. | 4. A dilated fundus examination was not performed. | 5. The patient was referred urgently for consultation by a retina specialist. | 9. A, Fundus photograph of the right eye demonstrating multifocal patches of inner retinal whitening in the posterior pole. | 11. B, Optical coherence tomography through the macula demonstrating mild intraretinal cystoid abnormalities and hyperreflective thickened areas in the nerve fiber and inner nuclear layer, corresponding to the white retinal patches.

1. A man in his 80s presented with a 1-year history of purpura, ecchymoses, anorexia, and weight loss. | 2. His medical history included alcohol abuse and cognitive impairment. | 3. Purpura and ecchymoses, initially periorbital, progressed over the previous 12 months. | 5. Examination demonstrated waxy yellow papules and plaques with purpura in the periocular, neck, axillary, trunk, and inguinal regions (Figure, A). | 6. 1. A 19-year-old man presented with recurrent left eye redness and photophobia for the past year. | 2. The patient had previously been treated with topical corticosteroid therapy, which provided temporary relief of his symptoms. | 3. Visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal intraocular pressures. | 4. The results from the slitlamp examination of the right eye were within normal limits (Figure 1A). | 5. Examination results of the left eye demonstrated 2+ diffuse conjunctival hyperemia, 1+ anterior chamber cell, and a vascularized iris infiltrate (Figure 1B). | 6. Results of the dilated fundus examination were within normal limits in both eyes. | 7. Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the left eye demonstrated areas of ciliary body thickening 360° and a thickened iris pupillary margin superiorly and nasally. | 8. A full review of systems was negative for other abnormalities including skin lesions. | 9. Test results for tuberculosis and syphilis were negative.

1. An 81-year-old woman presented with a 30 cm-wide, easily bleeding, violaceous, cutaneous lesion of the left scapular region with a superinfected necrotic central portion surrounded by satellite telangiectatic papules (Figure, A). | 2. The patient first noticed a rapidly expanding, itchy, painful nodule, which measured 3 cm in diameter, 5 months prior to presentation (Figure, B). | 3. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed only a left adrenal gland mass, consistent with adenoma. | 8. On physical examination, there were no other cutaneous lesions though multiple ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes, and enlarged supraclavicular and cervical lymph nodes were present. | 9. All other physical and laboratory findings were unremarkable. | 10. A skin punch biopsy of the lesion was obtained (Figure, C).

1. A 56-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-week history of worsening neck and shoulder pain. | 3. He had no history of recent trauma. | 4. He admitted to paresthesia and pain radiating down his right arm but denied any weakness. | 5. He had no difficulty with speech or swallowing. | 6. No palpable lymphadenopathy, swelling, or mass was noted. | 10. 1. A 35-year-old man presented after experiencing a 5-minute episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizure 3 days earlier. | 2. No other accompanying symptoms were reported. | 3. He had experienced painless decrease of vision in both eyes for 6 years but did not seek medical care. | 4. He had had hypertension for 3 years, with amlodipine taken regularly. | 5. A sibling developed uremia in their 30s. | 6. A parent died of kidney failure in their 40s. | 7. 1. At birth, a full-term newborn was noted to have numerous hypopigmented skin macules on the trunk, scalp, neck, face, back, and limbs after an uncomplicated pregnancy (Figure 1A). | 2. The family history was negative for any dermatologic or genetic diseases. | 3. A shave biopsy specimen of the right leg was interpreted as papillomatous epidermal hyperplasia consistent with an epidermal nevus. | 4. Because of the constellation of findings, an initial diagnosis of linear epidermal nevus syndrome was made. | 5. At age 3 months, the patient was referred for ophthalmologic examination owing to a flat, hypopigmented lesion in the left temporal iris noted by the patient’s father. | 8. Dilated ophthalmoscopic examination revealed a well-demarcated hypopigmented lesion originating from the retinal nerve fiber layer and protruding into the vitreous cavity of the right eye (Figure 1B). | 9. A similar lesion was seen along the left inferotemporal arcade (Figure 1C). | 10. B-scan ultrasonography revealed a 4.0 × 2.9 × 2.2-mm lesion with no calcification, no retinal detachment, and no choroidal involvement (Figure 1D). | 11. Given the suspected iris hamartoma and retinal astrocytic hamartoma, a systemic workup was commenced.A, Dermatologic manifestations. | 12. The patient had multiple hypopigmented macules on his scalp, face, neck, back, limbs, and torso (arrowheads). | 13. B, A lesion was discovered in the right eye consistent with a retinal astrocytic hamartoma. | 14. C, A similar smaller lesion was seen in the left eye. | 15. D, B-scan ultrasonography revealed an elevated lesion emanating from the retina with no calcification or choroidal involvement.

1. A 51-year-old man diagnosed as having acute promyelocytic leukemia, undergoing induction therapy with all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA) and arsenic trioxide that were started 2 weeks prior, presented with sudden loss of vision. | 2. Hospital course was complicated by neutropenic fever, receiving cefepime, acyclovir, vancomycin, and voriconazole for prophylaxis. | 3. Laboratory test results were remarkable for pancytopenia. | 4. On initial examination, his visual acuity was count fingers at 3 ft in both eyes. | 5. Intraocular pressures were 10 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. | 6. Pupils were round and reactive without a relative afferent pupillary defect. | 7. Color plates were 1 of 8 OU, with 50% brightness desaturation in the right eye and no red desaturation. | 8. Extraocular movements were full. | 9. Slitlamp examination was negative for any signs of inflammation. | 10. Dilated fundus examination demonstrated bilateral choroidal effusions with diffuse serous retinal detachments (RD) involving the macula without vitritis as well as white centered intraretinal hemorrhages along peripapillary and superior and inferior arcade distributions in both eyes (Figure, A). | 11. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated irregular inner retinal surface and subretinal fluid with septae with loss of the ellipsoid zone (Figure, B). | 12. Review of systems was positive for fever, tachycardia, odynophagia, productive cough with wheezing, and marked peripheral edema in upper extremities and negative for headache, nausea, vomiting, dysacusis, meningismus, or skin changes.Fundus photographs and optical coherence tomography 4 days from presentation demonstrating bilateral choroidal effusions with serous retinal detachment and white centered intraretinal hemorrhages. | 13. Left eye results shown. | 14. A, Left eye color fundus photograph demonstrates peripheral choroidal effusion with areas of stippled subretinal fluid in the macula, areas of intraretinal hemorrhages scattered throughout the posterior pole as well as far temporal periphery. | 15. B, Optical coherence tomography of the left eye demonstrating corrugated inner retina with intraretinal and subretinal fluid with septae from further separation of the external limiting membrane and ellipsoid zone as well as some loss of the ellipsoid zone.

1. A Japanese man in his 50s presented with a 6-month history of worsening pruritic hand dermatitis that progressed to involve his face, trunk, upper extremities, and feet. | 2. He had emigrated from Japan more than 10 years earlier but had no history of recent travel. | 3. He took no medications, had no significant medical or surgical history, and denied personal and family history of atopy. | 4. While he worked as a biomedical researcher, he denied any caustic exposures. | 5. On physical examination, his face, trunk, upper extremities, palms, and soles were marked by 1- to 2-mm erythematous papules and pustules coalescing into large, partially indurated and polycyclic plaques with centrifugal extension and occasional central clearing (Figure, A and B). | 6. Treatment with potent topical corticosteroids was ineffective. | 7. Punch biopsies of lesions on the shoulder (Figure, C) and foot (Figure, D) were performed.A, Annular erythematous plaque studded with papules and pustules on the cheek and temple. | 8. B, Erythematous plaques studded with papules and pustules on the shoulder. | 9. C and D, Lesional specimens under hematoxylin-eosin stain taken from the shoulder (C, original magnification ×400) and plantar foot (D, original magnification ×40).

1. A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department with chest pain. | 2. He states that the pain is dull in quality, started 30 minutes ago, has been gradually worsening, and is worse with exertion. | 3. He also endorses some shortness of breath. | 4. He also believes the pain is worse when leaning back and improved when leaning forward. | 5. His wife noticed he fainted after the pain started but regained consciousness shortly after. | 6. He has a medical history of diabetes and hypertension for which he is on metformin and losartan. | 7. His temperature is 99.2°F (37.3°C), blood pressure is 130/87 mmHg, pulse is 99/min, respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. | 9. A normal S1 and S2 are auscultated with clear breath sounds.

1. A 13-year-old boy with a longstanding history of gait imbalance presented with 2 episodes of acute-onset left hemibody weakness and dysarthria without changes in sensorium in a 24-hour period. | 2. Symptoms lasted approximately 60 minutes each before completely resolving; prior to the day of the events, he had never experienced similar phenomena. | 3. Initial examination following the second event revealed mild-to-moderate dysarthria, pes planovalgus and tight achilles tendons bilaterally, and decreased vibratory and fine touch sensation from the great toe up to the mid shin bilaterally. | 4. Reflexes were absent at the patella and achilles bilaterally. | 5. Bilateral dorsiflexion weakness was present (4 of 5). | 6. There were otherwise no motor deficits, muscle atrophy, or lateralizing neurologic abnormalities. | 8. Results of a comprehensive metabolic panel, complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and a coagulation panel were within normal limits. | 9. Computed tomography angiogram demonstrated no evidence of extra or intracranial dissection. | 10. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with and without contrast (Figure) demonstrated symmetric, bilateral, restricted diffusion, with T2 hyperintensities in the supratentorial white matter and corpus callosum. | 11. Lumbar puncture was obtained and revealed normal cell counts and no oligoclonal bands or evidence of infection. | 13. B, T2 sequence demonstrating bilateral and symmetric increased signal in the supratenorial white matter–sparing U-fibers. | 14. The patient had reportedly always walked on the outside of his feet and had been considered clumsy when compared with other children but had no history of motor delays. | 15. Family history revealed a mother with diminished reflexes, hand tremor, and balance issues with a prior inconclusive electromyogram and nerve conduction study. | 16. A younger brother with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder also had similar gait abnormalities.

1. A man in his 30s with an unremarkable medical and ocular history presented to his optometrist with reduced peripheral vision. | 2. The patient reported slowly progressive difficulty with night driving as well as perceiving objects in the periphery over the past 5 years. | 3. The patient was an avid basketball player and was forced to quit recently when he was unable to locate his teammates during play. | 4. He denied changes in color vision. | 5. There was no history of trauma. | 6. He did not use tobacco, alcohol, or drugs. | 7. His parents and both siblings were reportedly healthy with no history of ocular disease. | 8. His visual acuity was 20/20 OU, with no afferent pupillary defect. | 9. The Farnsworth D-15 dichotomous test results were normal in the right eye and tritan deficient in the left eye. | 12. His anterior examination results were unremarkable with no evidence of intraocular inflammation. | 13. The dilated fundus examination results showed minimal optic nerve pallor, vascular attenuation in both eyes, and a subtle area of increased pigmentation in the superior retina of the right eye only (Figure 1A). | 14. The fundus autofluorescence results showed bilateral peripheral mottled hypoautofluorescence contrasting a ring of hyperautofluorescence around the macula (Figure 1B). | 15. Automated perimetry was reliable and showed symmetrical severe bilateral field constriction with a remaining island of 6° of central vision. | 17. A, Widefield photograph (Optos) showing vascular attenuation, with reduced vessel caliber in the macula (asterisks) and vessels sclerosis in the periphery (black arrowhead). | 18. There is a small area of hyperpigmentation in midperiphery just superior to the optic nerve (white arrowhead). | 19. B, Fundus autofluorescence image showing peripheral hypoautofluorescence, with mottling in the midperiphery (particularly nasally) contrasting a ring of hyperautofluorescence in the macula.

1. A 34-year-old female Jehovah’s Witness presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of colicky lower abdominal pain, nausea without vomiting, and constipation after passing a single small bloody bowel movement. | 2. Physical examination demonstrated a soft, nontender, and nondistended abdomen without peritoneal signs or palpable masses. | 3. Digital rectal examination revealed no stool in the vault and gross blood and pelvic examination were negative. | 4. Surgical history was notable only for a previous cesarean delivery. | 5. Medical history was significant for 2 years of waxing and waning generalized abdominal pain and a hospital admission for small-bowel obstruction 11 months prior that was managed conservatively. | 6. Endoscopic evaluation revealed multiple polyps in the colon, stomach, and duodenum consistent with a diagnosis of juvenile polyposis syndrome. | 7. Admission laboratories demonstrated a lactate level of 18 mg/dL (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.111), white blood cell count of 6000/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001), and hemoglobin level of 13.3 g/dL (to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10). | 8. Amylase and lipase levels and chemistry findings were normal. | 9. Computed tomography with oral and intravenous contrast was obtained and is shown with imaging from her initial presentation 11 months prior (Figure 1). | 10. Axial and coronal views of computed tomography imaging on initial presentation (A) and 1 year later (B).

1. A woman in her late 20s presented with an asymptomatic hyperpigmentation on the right side of the trunk, right upper arm, and right leg, strictly following the lines of Blaschko (Figure, A and B). | 2. A slight atrophy of the hyperpigmented skin was palpable without any signs of induration. | 3. Clinical images show slightly atrophic hyperpigmented macules following the lines of Blaschko on the right side of the (A) trunk and (B) upper arm. | 4. Histopathologic images of punch biopsy specimen show (C) normal epidermis and dermis with a slight hyperpigmentation of the basal epidermis layer (hematoxylin-eosin stain), and (D) preserved elastic fibers in the reticular dermis (Elastic van Gieson stain). | 5. The first onset was in her childhood, at the age of 6 years, with a small hyperpigmentation on the right side of her lower chest remaining stable for years. | 6. In her early 20s the area of hyperpigmentation started to spread slowly over the above-mentioned areas and became more and more intense. | 7. Intravenous penicillin G therapy with 10 million units 3 times daily over 1 week combined with a UV-A1 phototherapy in 18 sessions with a maximum dose of 40 J/cm2 and a cumulative overall dose of 670 J/cm2 showed no effects. | 8. A punch biopsy was obtained (Figure, C and D).

1. A man in his 30s with no medical history reported a 2-year history of waxing and waning pruritic papules involving his left popliteus, contralateral popliteus, groin, and penis with each lesion occurring at different time points. | 2. He was initially evaluated by an infectious disease physician and a local dermatologist, who had intermittently prescribed empirical antibiotics (clindamycin hydrochloride and doxycycline calcium) for a presumptive clinical diagnosis of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection for more than 1 year with minimal response. | 3. Because no objective data including wound culture or biopsy were obtained during his prior evaluations, he sought an alternate clinical consultation given the appearance of new violaceous ulcerated lesions over his right lateral proximal calf (Figure, A) despite his actively taking doxycycline. | 4. He endorsed spontaneous healing of previously involved sites despite the absence of antibiotic exposure but denied constitutional complaints, recent travel, or high-risk behavior. | 5. His physical examination was unremarkable for hepatosplenomegaly or systemic adenopathy. | 6. Laboratory evaluation including complete blood cell count, peripheral blood cultures, MRSA swab, human immunodeficiency virus/human T-cell lymphotropic virus testing, flow cytometry, and Lyme disease titers had unremarkable results. | 7. Pathologic sampling of the lesions revealed V-shaped perifascicular infiltrative large lymphocytes with abundant amphophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli (Figure, B and C). | 8. Lesional cells exclusively involving the dermis stained positive for CD30, leukocyte common antigen, CD2, TIA-1, and CD4 and negative for CD7, CD8, CD43, CD56, and programmed cell death protein 1. | 9. Scattered B lymphocytes were PAX5 positive and CD20 positive. | 10. Ki-67 level was 87%. | 11. Scattered dermal dendritic and Langerhans cells were S100 positive. | 13. Systemic imaging did not reveal extracutaneous involvement, and screening endoscopy for upper and lower gastrointestinal involvement had unremarkable results.A, Photograph of right lateral proximal calf shows violaceous ulcerated nodule. | 14. B and C, Biopsy of the lesion revealed V-shaped perifascicular infiltrative large lymphocytes with abundant amphophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli hematoxlyn-eosin, original magnification ×2 and ×20, respectively).

1. A man in his 50s with a history of smoking and chronic hypertension was admitted to our hospital with a 36-hour history of upper abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. | 2. He had no history of previous surgery or trauma. | 3. His systolic blood pressure was 109 mm Hg, his diastolic blood pressure was 70 mm Hg, and his pulse rate was 100 beats/min. | 4. A physical examination revealed moderate epigastric tenderness with rebound and guarding. | 5. Laboratory test results were remarkable for a white blood cell count of 13 970/μL, hemoglobin level of 8.4 g/dL, serum creatinine level of 1.67 mg/dL, serum amylase level of 57 U/L (reference range, 30-110 U/L), and serum triglyceride level of 282.42 mg/dL, with no evidence of coagulopathy. (To convert the white blood cell count to ×109 per liter, multiply by 0.001; hemoglobin level to grams per liter, by 10; serum creatinine level to micromoles per liter, by 88.4; serum amylase level to microkatals per liter, by 0.0167; and serum triglyceride level to millimoles per liter, by 0.0113.) Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) and mesenteric angiography were performed (Figure 1).A, Contrast-enhanced computed tomographic (CECT) image showing an intra-abdominal hyperdense mass (arrowhead) and free fluid in the upper abdomen. | 6. B, Visceral artery angiogram revealing an aneurysm (arrowhead).

1. A man in his 50s reported a 4-week history of intermittent blurry vision in the right eye. | 2. Review of systems was positive for a skin rash on the upper arms and trunk, which he noticed 2 months earlier. | 3. Medical history included well-controlled type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and sitagliptin. | 4. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU. | 5. There was a barely perceptible right relative afferent pupillary defect. | 6. Anterior segment examination was normal. | 7. On ophthalmoscopy, there were few vitreous cells with no detectable haze and optic nerve head edema grade IV on the Frisén scale, with peripapillary flame hemorrhages in the right eye (Figure); the optic nerve was normal on the left. | 8. Automated perimetry using the 24-2 pattern and Swedish interactive threshold algorithm strategy (Humphrey Field Analyzer; Carl Zeiss Meditec) was normal in each eye and optical coherence tomography showed marked elevation of the peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer on the right. | 9. The remainder of the neurological examination was normal. | 10. Fundus picture of the right eye demonstrating optic nerve head edema with peripapillary flame hemorrhages.

1. A woman in her 70s with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and venous thromboembolism presented to the hospital with 2 months of progressively worsening dyspnea on exertion. | 2. Her medical history was significant for a single episode of lower-extremity deep venous thrombosis during a prior hospitalization, complicated by multiple subsegmental pulmonary emboli. | 5. She denied any substantial tobacco or alcohol use, and her family history was negative for venous thromboembolic disease. | 6. Her initial physical examination had unremarkable results, with laboratory evaluation of prothrombin time significant for an international normalized ratio of 2.8. | 7. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed a large filling defect within the main pulmonary artery, flattening of the interventricular septum, and multiple pulmonary nodules. | 8. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated evidence of severely increased right ventricular systolic pressure, with moderate right ventricular dilation. | 9. She was referred for urgent pharmacomechanical interventions, including catheter-directed embolectomy and thrombolysis, for a presumed diagnosis of submassive pulmonary embolism. | 10. Following the procedure, she experienced no substantial clinical or radiographic improvement.

1. A 33-year-old woman with a history of hereditary bilateral retinoblastoma as an infant presented to a primary care clinic with 1 week of right lower extremity swelling. | 2. At age 8 months, she was treated with right enucleation and left eye radiotherapy (50.4 Gy). | 3. At age 4 years, she developed a recurrence of the retinoblastoma in the nasal cavity and was treated with 4 cycles of vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide followed by 1 cycle of cisplatin, etoposide, and intrathecal cytarabine. | 4. Primary care evaluation was prompted by her mother, as the patient had not noticed her lower extremity edema. | 5. She had no fevers, weight loss, shortness of breath, chest pain, abdominal pain, or history of deep vein thrombosis. | 6. Her physical examination was notable for firm, nonpitting edema to the hip. | 7. She did not have any associated tenderness, inguinal lymphadenopathy, or palpable abdominal masses. | 9. Laboratory work results, including a complete blood cell count with a differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and D-dimer levels, were within normal limits. | 10. Doppler ultrasonography of her right lower extremity showed no deep vein thrombosis. | 11. A computed tomography venogram demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.5 cm mass of likely vascular origin that was extending into the right common iliac vein (Figure). | 12. Computed tomography venogram demonstrating a 4.0 × 3.5 cm heterogeneously enhancing lobulated mass (arrowhead) extending into the right common iliac vein.

1. A man in his 70s with hypertension, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) presented for a second opinion regarding treatment of MDS. | 2. Three years prior he had developed neutropenia and mild thrombocytopenia. | 3. A bone marrow biopsy sample demonstrated refractory cytopenia with multilineage dysplasia. | 4. Cytogenetic testing results were normal, and there were 5% bone marrow blasts. | 7. After approximately 2 years, he developed more pronounced cytopenias and presented with a white blood cell count of 2100/μL(480 neutrophils), hemoglobin level of 8.4 g/dL, and platelet count of 92 000/μL. | 8. He noted fatigue, but otherwise felt well. | 9. Physical examination revealed an isolated, symptomatic polypoid mass involving his right upper labial mucosa (Figure). | 10. It had been recently biopsied without definitive diagnosis, but since the biopsy, the mass had increased in size.

1. A 53-year-old man developed patchy numbness in his right arm. | 2. The numbness progressed over 10 months to involve his entire right arm, patches of his left arm, and his distal lower extremities. | 3. He also developed right-hand incoordination and imbalance. | 5. A complete blood cell count with a differential; liver function testing; tests for HIV, rapid plasma reagin, serum aquaporin-4 antibody, and antinuclear antibodies; and levels of sodium, calcium, creatinine, glucose, thyroxine, and vitamin B12 were unremarkable. | 6. Examinations of the cerebrospinal fluid had normal results twice, including for white blood cell count with a differential, glucose level, total protein level, IgG index, oligoclonal bands, cultures, and cytology testing.A, A brain coronal T1 postgadolinium magnetic resonance image (MRI), showing a lobulated heterogeneously enhancing mass in the brainstem and dural enhancement. | 7. B, A brain coronal T1 postgadolinium MRI from 10 months later with persistent yet evolving enhancement and mild size increase in brainstem lesion and ongoing dural enhancement.He sought neurological reconsultation 9 months later, reporting progressive blurred vision bilaterally, dysphagia, dysarthria, and urinary and bowel urgency. | 8. His gait had worsened, requiring a cane and, for 6 months, a walker. | 9. A physical examination was otherwise unremarkable, except for mild lower-extremity edema. | 10. A neurologic examination revealed decreased visual acuity (20/50 OU) with normal pupillary responses and discs; cerebellar dysarthria, dysmetria, and dysdiadochokinesia; and decreased proprioception in the toes with positive Romberg testing. | 11. He could not tandem walk. | 12. A follow-up brain MRI (Figure 1B) showed persistent enhancement plus bilateral optic nerve enhancement (not shown). | 13. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed infiltrative soft tissue in the pericardium and intra-atrial septum and throughout the retroperitoneum.

1. An 82-year-old woman presented with dyspnea on exertion and weight gain of 5 kg over the past month. | 2. Her medical history included atrial fibrillation and lung adenocarcinoma (a lung lobectomy was performed 8 years ago). | 3. Her blood pressure was 112/60 mm Hg, her heart rate was 100 beats per minute, her respiratory rate was 37 breaths per minute, her body temperature was 36.6°C, and her oxygen saturation was 100% while breathing 10 L of oxygen. | 4. A cardiac examination was clinically significant for an irregular rhythm, an increased pulmonic closure sound, and jugular venous distension. | 5. Bibasilar coarse crackles and pretibial edema were also noted. | 6. A complete blood count had results within normal limits. | 7. The serum lactate dehydrogenase level was 278 U/L (to convert to microkatal per liter, multiply by 0.0167). | 8. A chest radiographic image showed bibasilar infiltrates. | 9. An electrocardiogram was notable for atrial fibrillation, and echocardiography revealed normal left ventricular function, mild right atrial and ventricular dilatation, and severe tricuspid regurgitation (transtricuspid pressure gradient, 40 mm Hg). | 10. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography image revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities and right basilar consolidations, with no evidence of thromboembolisms (Figure, A). | 11. Para-aortic and inguinal lymphadenopathies were also noted. | 12. Presumptive diagnoses of pulmonary hypertension (PH) and right-sided heart failure were made. | 13. The patient began receiving dobutamine and furosemide, but she continuously required 2 to 10 L of oxygen, and further invasive evaluations could not be performed. | 14. An echocardiogram identified aggravating PH (transtricuspid pressure gradient, 57 mm Hg). | 15. A thorough physical examination identified scaly, crusty genital skin lesions pathologically compatible with extramammary Paget disease. | 17. An autopsy was performed (Figure, B).A, The chest computed tomography showed ground-glass opacities (white arrowheads) and consolidative lesions (a yellow arrowhead), but no evidence of thromboembolism was obtained. | 18. B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of the lung showed proliferation of intimal fibromuscular cells with (yellow arrowheads) or without (black arrowheads) the presence of Paget cells. | 19. Yellow arrowheads show embolized Paget cells. | 20. The encircled area (black arrowheads) indicates the vascular lumen, the inside of which is filled with proliferated fibromuscular cells but not Paget cells (original magnification ×400).

1. A 3-week-old boy presents to the emergency department with vomiting. | 2. His parents report that he suddenly started vomiting this morning and has shown no interest in feeding since then. | 3. They describe the vomitus as green and without any traces of blood. | 5. He was noted to have surpassed his birth weight at his last office visit 1 week ago. | 6. His temperature is 97.6°F (36.4°C), blood pressure is 78/56 mmHg, pulse is 148/min, and respirations are 44/min. | 7. On physical exam, the patient is in mild distress. | 8. He has no dysmorphic features, and his mucous membranes are dry. | 9. His abdomen is soft and distended. | 10. Bowel sounds are hypoactive. | 11. An abdominal radiograph is performed as in Figure A.

1. A 70-year-old woman with hypertension, atrial fibrillation, congestive heart failure, and gallstones presented to the emergency department with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. | 2. She reported no hematemesis, hematochezia, or melena and had no history of abdominal surgery. | 3. On admission to the emergency department, she was afebrile, her blood pressure was 80/60 mm Hg, and heart rate was 122/min. | 4. On physical examination, her abdomen was distended, tympanic, and slightly tender to palpation diffusely. | 5. Blood testing showed a white blood cell count of 10 450/μL (84.1% neutrophils); C-reactive protein level, 9.5 mg/dL; potassium level, 3.0 mEq/L (reference, 3.6-5.2 mEq/L); and creatinine level, 5.57 mg/dL (429.39 μmol/L, up from a baseline level of 0.80 mg/dL [70.72 μmol/L]). | 6. Sodium and liver function values were normal. | 7. In the emergency department, she received a 500-mL bolus of intravenous crystalloid fluid and 1 g of intravenous ceftriaxone. | 8. A nasogastric tube was placed and initially drained 300 mL of biliary fluid. | 10. Left, Abdominal computed tomography scan showing a thickened gallbladder with air and gallstones adherent to the duodenum, with a suspected fistula tract. | 11. Right, Axial section showing a 2.7-cm gallstone in the middle ileum and proximal bowel distension. | 12. Administer barium through the nasogastric tube to evaluate for bowel obstruction Plan for surgical intervention after intravenous fluid resuscitation in the intensive care unit (ICU)

1. A man in his 60s presented with a 3-month history of intertrigo involving his groin that he had been treating with a combination of clotrimazole cream, 1%, and hydrocortisone cream, 1%. | 2. His intertrigo improved, but he then developed bright red, burning and painful nodules around his scrotum (Figure 1). | 3. His medical history included prostate cancer, hypertension, anxiety disorder, hyperlipidemia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and diverticulosis. | 4. His medications included omeprazole, alprazolam, amlodipine besylate, atenolol, simvastatin, and valsartan. | 5. On physical examination, there were 2 symmetrical solitary erythematous nodules in the right and left inguinal folds adjacent to the scrotum. | 6. Clinical image of well-demarcated erythematous solitary papule in the right inguinal fold.

1. A 53-year-old woman with a history of stage IVA1 (T4N1M0B2) mycosis fungoides presented with a new 1-month history of hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa (Figure 1). | 2. Examination of the mouth revealed multiple coalescing painless nonpruritic black macules and patches on the tongue, roof of the mouth, and buccal mucosa. | 3. Examination of the skin was notable for erythematous and hyperpigmented patches covering 90% of the body surface area, consistent with her known mycosis fungoides. | 4. Other notable findings on examination were 1- to 2-cm lymphadenopathy in the bilateral inguinal folds and axillae. | 5. Review of systems was notable for fatigue. | 6. The patient had previously received 5 cycles of romidepsin with progression of disease, followed by 4 doses of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin hydrochloride, which was followed by partial response.

1. A young man presented to the emergency department with a 1-day history of vision loss in the left eye. | 2. He had experienced eye redness for 1 week, which resolved with use of artificial tears; a mild posterior headache; and paresthesias of the left thumb and index and middle fingers. | 3. His medical history was significant for epilepsy as a child, although he had been seizure free for more than 10 years without medication. | 7. His best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/100 OS. | 8. Amsler grid testing revealed a central scotoma in the left eye. | 9. No afferent papillary defect was apparent. | 10. Intraocular pressures were 16 mm Hg OU. | 11. Results of the external and anterior segment examinations were unremarkable, and no vitreous inflammation was noted. | 12. Figure 1 shows findings of the posterior segment examination. | 13. Results of the neurologic examination revealed decreased sensation to light touch, vibration, and temperature in his left upper and lower extremities. | 14. A, Subretinal and retinal pigment epithelial lesions (arrowheads) are visible in the left eye. | 15. B, Late staining of the macular lesion. | 16. The arrowheads outline the border of the area that was hypofluorescent in the early frames (not shown). | 17. The right eye showed similar findings.

1. A 27-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for an abnormal vaginal discharge. | 2. The patient has engaged in unprotected intercourse with 12 different partners. | 3. She has a medical history of asthma, IV drug abuse, and depression. | 5. She feels ashamed of her behavior and is requesting treatment for her condition and advice for safe sex. | 6. The patient is given antibiotics and is advised on safe sex practices. | 7. The patient presents to the emergency department 3 days later with a complaint of a rash. | 8. She states that every time she has sex a rash has emerged on her skin. | 10. A physical exam is notable for the finding in Figure A.

1. A woman in her 60s presented for evaluation of multiple painful cutaneous nodules that had developed over the previous 2 months. | 2. The patient had a history of IgGκ multiple myeloma, diagnosed approximately 6 months earlier. | 3. At that time, flow cytometry showed a κ-restricted plasma cell population positive for CD38 and CD138 but negative for CD3, CD20, and CD45 expression. | 4. Cytogenetic analysis with fluorescent in situ hybridization did not reveal high-risk genetic markers. | 5. The patient demonstrated no evidence of end organ disease, and her myeloma was classified as stage II. | 6. Since her initial diagnosis, she had completed 4 cycles of lenalidomide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (RVD) therapy in addition to irradiation for lytic lesions of the thoracic and lumbar spine. | 7. Physical examination revealed scattered red-violaceous nodules, with the largest measuring approximately 6.0 × 5.5 × 2.5 cm (Figure, A). | 8. They were found in the mouth, the trunk, and on all 4 extremities. | 9. The lesions were nonulcerated, round with a smooth surface, fixed, and firm and tender to touch. | 10. Serum protein levels were normal.
1. A 2-week-old boy is evaluated by his pediatrician for abnormal feet. | 7. A musculoskeletal exam reveals the findings shown in Figure A.

1. A 62-year-old woman with a history of chronic angle-closure glaucoma and bilateral peripheral iridotomies sought a second opinion for worsening visual acuity in the left eye for 2 months. | 2. She had been treated for glaucoma for approximately 1 year. | 3. Review of systems was negative for previous episodes of eye pain, redness, or emesis. | 4. Her medical history included hyperlipidemia, obesity, and prior cataract surgery in both eyes. | 5. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/80 OS. | 6. The patient’s pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light without a relative afferent pupillary defect. | 7. Intraocular pressure was 11 mm Hg bilaterally without medication. | 8. A dacryocystogram of the left lacrimal system indicated partial dacryostenosis, but compression of the canaliculi and lacrimal sac did not exacerbate discharge. | 6. A prior computed tomography scan of the orbits and sinuses showed no abnormalities. | 7. Her visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/100 OS. | 8. Deep superior conjunctival fornices were noted in both eyes (Figure 1), and eversion of the left upper eyelid revealed a pseudomembrane of the tarsal conjunctiva. | 9. Cultures of the copious discharge demonstrated many gram-negative Serratia marcescens. | 10. She subsequently started treatment with topical prednisolone acetate, moxifloxacin, and systemic azithromycin. | 12. Two weeks after the initial consultation, the patient reported persistent but improved symptoms in the left eye. | 13. At this follow-up visit, her visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/200 OS.

1. A 30-year-old man was referred with progressive quadriplegia for 2 months. | 2. The muscle weakness started from the right lower limb and gradually spread to the upper limb and contralateral side. | 3. Urinary retention developed 1 month later. | 4. Because he was suspected of having tubercular meningomyelitis, he received an antituberculosis regimen plus dexamethasone (10 mg daily) for 10 days. | 5. The symptoms ameliorated in the first week but thereafter deteriorated with fever. | 6. He had no history of central nervous system injury or drug overuse. | 7. He was a construction supervisor and had daily contact with moist earth. | 9. On physical examination, he was alert and well oriented. | 10. The cranial nerve was intact, but he had quadriplegia with a Medical Research Council muscle scale grade of 0 of 5 power, decreased tendon reflexes, and bilateral positive Babinski sign. | 11. Pinprick and vibration sensation were markedly impaired below the nipples. | 12. Multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes could be palpitated. | 13. The skin was extraordinarily dry, and a pigmentation of 10 mm in diameter at the T2 vertebrae, just on the midline of the back, was noticed. | 14. Total blood T-cell count (CD3+) was 1643/uL (to convert to ×109 per liter, multiply by 0.001), and the patient had a CD4+/CD8+ ratio of 0.89. | 15. Results of blood testing for human immunodeficiency virus, syphilis, and tuberculosis were negative. | 16. Cerebrospinal fluid testing revealed pleocytosis (72 cells/uL; mononuclear cells, 59 of 72), elevated protein concentration (200 mg/dL), and a decreased glucose level (36.0 mg/dL [to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555]), but no organisms were identified on Gram stain or on stain for acid-fast bacilli. | 17. Pulmonary computed tomography showed enlarged lymph nodes in mediastinum and axillary regions. | 18. Results from magnetic resonance imaging of the brain were normal, while magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine revealed multiple intramedullary lesions with enhancement (Figure 1).Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine. | 19. Multiple intramedullary lesions and enlarged lymph nodes with strong enhancement were revealed. | 21. The subcutaneous abscess beneath the pigmentation on the back is also shown.

1. A man in his 30s was referred to the retina clinic with a diagnosis of bilateral branch retinal vein occlusions. | 2. He reported flashes and progressive blurry vision in both eyes over a period of 6 days. | 3. He had no history of eye problems. | 4. His medical history was negative for diabetes and hypertension, and review of systems was positive for recent easy bruising and progressive fatigue. | 6. Results from examination of his pupils, motility, intraocular pressures, confrontational visual fields, and anterior segments were normal. | 7. A dilated fundus examination was conducted (Figure). | 8. He had bilateral flame-shaped and intraretinal hemorrhages in both maculae along the superior arcades and some scattered peripheral hemorrhages. | 9. There was no vessel tortuosity, and there were hard exudates in the left macula. | 10. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography showed areas of hyperreflectivity in the middle and outer retina. | 11. Fluorescein angiography of both eyes showed blocking in the areas of hemorrhage, good venous filling, no leakage, and no neovascularization.Wide-field scanning laser image of the left eye showed superficial and intraretinal hemorrhages and hard exudates.

1. A previously healthy 4-year-old girl with a history of prematurity (31 weeks’ gestational age) presented as a transfer from an outside facility with abdominal pain. | 2. She had presented to an outside emergency department 2 days prior with lower abdominal pain that subsequently localized to the right lower quadrant. | 3. Her pain was accompanied by anorexia and nonbloody, nonbilious emesis. | 4. She denied fevers or chills. | 5. She was noted to have voluntary guarding and focal right lower quadrant tenderness to palpation. | 6. Laboratory analyses demonstrated a mild leukocytosis (white blood cell count = 14 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]) and normal urinalysis results. | 7. Abdominal ultrasonography images were obtained that failed to show her appendix and demonstrated no secondary signs of inflammation. | 9. No antibiotics were initiated, and her activity improved with intravenous hydration. | 10. However, her right lower abdominal pain persisted, prompting further evaluation. | 12. She was transferred to our facility for surgical evaluation. | 13. In our emergency department, pelvic ultrasonography images were obtained that failed to show both the appendix and right adnexal structures.

1. A 69-year-old man with a history of relapsed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) monocytic type presented with intermittent fever and fatigue 2 months after allogeneic stem cell transplantation (SCT). | 2. Post-SCT bone marrow biopsy specimen analysis at day 30 showed no evidence of leukemic cells and 99.5% donor cells. | 3. His home medications included acyclovir, fluconazole, and cyclosporine. | 4. Temperature on admission was 103.1° F, and other vital signs were unremarkable. | 6. Complete blood cell counts with differential counts showed no evidence of peripheral blasts. | 7. Laboratory and imaging work-up—including chest radiographs, blood culture, fungal culture, urinalysis, sputum culture, respiratory viral panel, fungitell and galactomannan assay, coccidioidomycosis serology, and cytomegalovirus and human herpesvirus 6 polymerase chain reaction assays—were all negative. | 8. The patient was discharged with oral antibiotics after being afebrile for 72 hours. | 9. Thereafter, he had 2 more emergency department visits and was readmitted for recurrent fever. | 10. A thorough physical examination revealed 2 nonpruritic skin bumps on the right forearm and left calf that both measured 1.0 cm × 1.5 cm. | 11. Both bumps were soft without pigmentation or ulceration. | 12. Pathologic sampling of the respective lesions revealed a diffuse infiltration of large mononuclear cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio (Figure, A and B). | 13. Immunohistochemistry staining was positive for CD4 cells and myeloperoxidase (Figure, C and D)A and B, Histologic evaluation of the skin biopsy specimens.

1. An African American woman in her early to mid-60s presented to the ophthalmology clinic with complaints of flashes and occasional floaters in her left eye for the past 2 weeks. | 2. She had been seen 7 months prior to presentation for a comprehensive eye evaluation. | 3. She was found to have a bilateral posterior vitreous detachment, and the results of her retinal examination at that time were normal. | 4. Her best-corrected vision was 20/20 OU, and the intraocular pressure in each eye was normal. | 5. An anterior segment examination of the left eye revealed trace keratic precipitates on the inferior cornea and 1+ cell. | 6. A posterior segment examination revealed 1+ vitreous cell. | 7. A photograph from a fundus examination is shown in Figure 1. | 9. Color fundus photograph of the left eye demonstrating notably clear media and whitish-yellow periarterial lesions.

1. At that time, she was treated with a course of bendamustine and rituximab with subsequent maintenance treatment with rituximab for 2 years. | 5. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was performed, demonstrating T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensity in the left occipital and temporal lobes, crossing the corpus callosum and extending into the right occipital lobe without enhancement (Figure).A, Axial T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery precontrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain. | 6. 1. A 43-year-old construction worker experienced bilateral lower extremity crush injuries after a large heavy object fell onto his thighs, traumatically amputating his right leg. | 2. He was profoundly hypotensive (blood pressure, 70/40 mm Hg) and anemic (hemoglobin level, 5.6 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]) from extensive blood loss. | 4. He was urgently transfused and taken to the operating room for bilateral lower extremity irrigation and drainage and reconstruction of the left leg. | 5. Unfortunately, postoperative infection necessitated a left leg above-knee amputation. | 6. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit, intubated, and sedated for 1 month. | 7. On awakening, he reported that he was unable to see out of each eye. | 8. Bedside examination revealed no light perception vision with 7-mm pupils that were nonreactive bilaterally. | 9. Extraocular movements were full and there was no ptosis. | 10. Slitlamp examination findings were normal, and fundus photographs of the posterior pole in each eye are presented in the Figure. | 11. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain performed earlier in the hospitalization was normal. | 12. The patient was previously healthy and did not take any medications. | 13. Appearance of the optic nerves in fundus photographs taken 4 weeks after the patient’s injury at work. | 14. The optic discs are characterized by diffuse pallor, with no evidence of edema or hemorrhages. | 15. The remainder of the posterior pole, including macula and vessels, appear normal bilaterally.

1. A man with a 3-year history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presented with increasing dyspnea on exertion, requiring increasing flow rates of oxygen. | 2. He was a former smoker with a 50–pack-year history. | 3. He had been diagnosed with stage I low-grade prostate cancer several years previously. | 4. Lung examination showed no wheezing. | 5. Cardiac examination showed a prominent pulmonary component (P2) of the second heart sound. | 6. Noncontrast computed tomography of the chest was unremarkable. | 7. An echocardiogram revealed dilated right atrium and ventricle. | 8. Spirometry showed mild airway obstruction. | 9. Duplex ultrasound showed a nonocclusive thrombus in the left femoral and popliteal veins. | 10. Catheterization of the right side of the heart showed a pulmonary arterial pressure of 79/32 mm Hg (mean, 48 mm Hg) with a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.

The parents reported occasional erosions and crusting that resolved with topical mupirocin, 2%, cream, but with no continued growth. | 4. Physical examination revealed a firm, exophytic, and flat-topped nodule, with superficial erosion and crust on the right parietal side of the scalp measuring 3 cm in diameter and 1 cm thick (Figure, A). | 5. No other skin lesions were found. | 8. The lesion regressed without treatment over a period of 8 months. | 9. Close follow-up every 3 months was scheduled, and complete involution of the tumor was noted at 10 months of age (Figure, D). | 13. D, Complete regression of tumor at 10 months of age.

1. A 32-year-old G1P0 woman delivers a boy at 40 weeks and 3 days of gestation. | 2. The delivery is uncomplicated and the neonate has Apgar scores of 9 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes respectively. | 3. After 15 minutes, he attempts to nurse for the 1st time. | 4. His mother notices that his face, chest, and extremities turn dusky blue during nursing. | 5. She also notes that he seems to be snoring loudly and breathing very quickly. | 6. When she removes him from her breast, he begins to cry and his color improves. | 7. His temperature is 98.2°F (36.7°C), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 45/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air.

1. A 6-year-old girl was incidentally discovered to have fundus lesions after presenting with head trauma that resolved without permanent intracranial pathology. | 2. She had no significant medical history or prior ocular problems. | 3. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/25 OS, with eccentric fixation and trace exophoria in the left eye. | 4. Pupils were equally round and reactive. | 5. Anterior segment examination revealed an enlarged right corneal nerve. | 6. The left macula had a fibrotic-appearing epiretinal membrane (Figure 1A). | 7. There were 2 small, flat, pigmented lesions along the arcades of the right fundus (Figure 1B), likely atypical congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) lesions, or pigmented ocular fundus lesions (POFLs). | 9. On follow-up, optical coherence tomography showed focal macular thickening in the left eye, most likely a retinal hamartoma (Figure 1C), and intraretinal abnormalities between the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor layer in the right eye, consistent with POFLs and likely representing combined retina-RPE hamartomas (Figure 1D). | 10. B-scan ultrasonography and biometric A-scan showed bilaterally clear vitreous without retinal detachment. | 12. There was no leakage or hyperfluorescence of the POFLs in the right eye (Figure 1F).

1. A 64-year-old man presented with 3 weeks of bilateral anterior uveitis unresponsive to treatment with topical steroids. | 2. He was referred to our clinic for worsening uveitis and ocular hypertension. | 3. The patient had no ocular history. | 4. His medical history was significant for 8 months of bilateral recurrent gingivitis with persistent reactive lymphadenopathy of the head and neck unresponsive to treatment with systemic antibiotics. | 5. He denied any constitutional symptoms. | 6. His visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/200 OS, and intraocular pressures were 17 and 32 mm Hg, respectively. | 7. On slitlamp examination, both eyes were markedly hyperemic with diffuse corneal stromal edema, and his anterior chambers were deep with 3+ OD and 4+ OS cell and mixed hypopyon and hyphema in each eye (Figure, A and B). | 8. His dilated fundus examination findings were remarkable only for an area of retinal pigment epithelial stippling inferonasal to the macula in the left eye, without any vitritis in either eye. | 9. He did not have any skin or mucocutaneous lesions, but he had extensive bilateral preauricular, submental, posterior occipital, and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. | 10. Gram stain and culture of aqueous and vitreous biopsy sample results were negative for infectious and cytologic studies, as were serum human leukocyte antigen B27, tuberculosis, syphilis, and sarcoidosis test results (Figure, C).Slitlamp examination findings of the left eye with hypopyon (A) and iris nodules (B). | 12. Note the scant cytoplasm containing small, irregular nuclei with inconspicuous nucleoli.

1. A 39-year-old woman had an acute onset of headache, increasing right-side hemiparesis, and numbness with fever. | 2. Computed tomography (CT) of the brain showed a ring-enhanced lesion with surrounding edema on the left frontoparietal lobe. | 3. Multiple red papules on the tongue (Figure 1), trunk, and limbs were noted during the physical examination. | 4. The patient stated she had not noticed the red papules before. | 5. There was no suggestion of otitis media or parasinusitis and no history of craniotomy, open head injury, or cyanotic heart disease. | 6. The patient did relate having many prior episodes of epistaxis since childhood. | 7. Blood cultures were obtained when the patient was first seen, and the patient received ampicillin/sulbactam empirically.

1. A 33-year-old man presents to the emergency department after slamming his finger in the car door 5 hours ago. | 2. He initially experienced pain which is currently well controlled with acetaminophen. | 5. Physical exam is notable for the finding in Figure A. | 6. A radiograph of the affected digits shows a smooth cortex without disruption of the bone.

1. A woman in her late 50s presented to the clinic with severe right eye pain and a headache for the past 2 days. | 2. Her ophthalmic history was significant for mixed-mechanism glaucoma due to uveitis and chronic angle closure with prior implantation of bilateral superotemporal Baerveldt drainage implants. | 4. In addition, she had Fuchs corneal dystrophy. | 5. A month earlier, she had undergone Baerveldt implant repositioning from the anterior chamber to the sulcus in the right eye in preparation for future Descemet stripping endothelial keratoplasty owing to severe corneal decompensation. | 6. At that time, visual acuity was counting fingers at 1 ft OD. | 8. On the first postoperative visit, IOP was 14 mm Hg OD by Goldmann applanation. | 9. On postoperative day 11, IOP remained stable at 7 mm Hg OD by Goldmann applanation and topical atropine was discontinued. | 10. At presentation 3 weeks postoperatively, IOP was 30 mm Hg OD by Goldmann applanation. | 11. Her visual acuity worsened from counting fingers to hand motions. | 12. Slitlamp examination of the right eye revealed a superotemporal Baerveldt drainage implant with fluid over the plate. | 14. White arrowheads indicate the anterior and posterior borders of the tube; magenta arrowhead, the lumen of the tube; AC, anterior chamber; and C, cornea.

1. A 60-year-old man with advanced melanoma presented with headaches and increasing fatigue during treatment with ipilimumab. | 2. Several months earlier, he presented to the emergency department with shortness of breath. | 3. Imaging revealed pulmonary emboli and incidental groin lymphadenopathy. | 4. Biopsy of a lymph node showed melanoma. | 5. He then underwent inguinal lymph node dissection and was found to have 9 lymph nodes involved with melanoma (stage IIIC melanoma).He was then treated with ipilimumab (3 mg/kg), a monoclonal antibody to cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4), every 3 weeks, as part of an investigational adjuvant therapy clinical trial. | 6. When presenting for his fourth and final dose of ipilimumab, he reported central headaches, severe fatigue, poor appetite, intermittent nausea, and a mild rash. | 7. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits. | 8. Physical examination had largely unremarkable results except for a slightly red, raised rash over his chest and proximal extremities.Laboratory testing showed the following: thyrotropin, 0.02 mIU/L (reference range, 0.3-5.0 mIU/L), and free thyroxine, less than 0.25 ng/dL (reference range, 0.5-1.2 ng/dL; to convert to picomoles per liter, multiply by 12.871). | 9. Cosyntropin stimulation test showed a cortisol peak level of 0.9 µg/dL (reference range, >20 µg/dL; to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 27.588). | 10. He had low corticotropin (<5 pg/mL; reference range, 7-51 pg/mL; to convert to picomoles per liter, multiply by 0.22) and testosterone levels (<0.1 ng/mL; reference range, 2-11 ng/mL; to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 0.0347). | 11. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is shown in the Figure.

1. A 71-year-old woman arrives to clinic with sudden vision loss. | 2. She was in her usual state of health until waking up this morning unable to see out of her right eye. | 3. She denies pain, but reports her right eye “feels funny.” The patient’s medical history is significant for a previous myocardial infarction, hypertension, and osteoporosis. | 4. Her current medications include aspirin, metoprolol, rosuvastatin, lisinopril, and alendronate. | 5. Her temperature is 98°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 145/86 mmHg, pulse is 62/min, and respirations are 12/min with an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. | 6. The patient's pupils are symmetric in size and equally reactive to light with accommodation. | 8. The left optic fundus is unremarkable.

1. An otherwise healthy 54-year-old woman presented with an erythematous right lower eyelid lesion with a vermiform appearance, accompanied by pruritus and pain (Figure 1A). | 2. The lesion resolved after 1 month, but she developed redness and swelling of the inner part of her right conjunctiva the next day (Figure 1B). | 3. She denied any vision changes, eye pain, eye discharge, or systemic symptoms, such as fevers, chills, night sweats, weight loss, or diarrhea. | 4. The patient had recently immigrated from rural Moldova 1 month prior to presentation, where she had exposure to farm animals, including dogs and cats. | 5. She had not traveled to any other countries. | 6. Painful and pruritic lower eyelid lesion with a vermiform appearance (arrow) (A). | 7. This was followed by an elevation in the bulbar conjunctiva with whitish linear opacities within the lesion (B). | 8. Ophthalmological examination showed a best-corrected visual acuity of 20/40 OU and intraocular pressures of 17 OD and 18 OS. | 9. Pupils were equal and reactive to light. | 10. On slit-lamp examination of the right eye, there was diffuse conjunctival vasodilation and hyperemia that was worse nasally. | 11. There was a cystic elevation of the bulbar conjunctiva nasally with whitish linear opacities within the lesion (Figure 1B). | 12. The cornea was clear. | 13. There was no anterior chamber or vitreous inflammation. | 14. Dilated fundus examination showed slightly anomalous appearing optic nerves; the macula and periphery were flat and attached without any lesions.

1. A 16-year-old male patient developed acute-onset right-sided periorbital swelling several days after being hit in that area by a snowball. | 2. The swelling worsened over the following 3 weeks despite use of warm compresses and a course of doxycycline prescribed by his outside eye care professionals. | 3. He had progressive binocular diplopia and right periorbital pain, swelling, and redness. | 4. Blurriness of the right eye that started the week before presentation eventually caused enough concern that the patient presented to his local emergency department where magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits revealed an intraconal mass (Figure, A). | 5. He then came to our institution’s emergency department for urgent ophthalmology consultation.A, Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) axial T1 orbit fat-suppressed postcontrast image shows a right retro-orbital intraconal lesion (asterisk) with intrinsic T1 hyperintensity but without fat saturation or enhancement. | 6. The lesion causes proptosis (difference between the dotted lines) and posterior globe flattening (white arrowheads). | 7. B, B-scan ultrasonography of the right eye shows a well-circumscribed and homogenous lesion with low internal reflectivity (asterisk) sitting directly behind the globe (left). | 8. There is a possible thin septation (white arrowheads).His examination revealed a visual acuity of 20/60 OD and 20/20 OS, intraocular pressures of 24 mm Hg and 17 mm Hg in the right and left eyes, respectively, and a normal pupil examination without a relative afferent pupillary defect. | 9. His right eye had 5-mm relative proptosis, hyperglobus, supraduction deficit, conjunctival injection, grade IV optic disc edema, and choroidal folds. | 10. An ultrasonography examination revealed a 2.0 × 2.5-cm echolucent avascular lesion (Figure, B). | 11. MRI of the orbits was reviewed by the on-call pediatric radiologist whose leading diagnosis was dermoid/epidermoid cyst.

1. A 64-year-old man was referred to our clinic for suspected central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) in his right eye. | 2. He had experienced blurred vision of the right eye for 2 months; medical history included hypercholesterolemia. | 3. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OD and 20/20 OS. | 4. The anterior segment was normal and intraocular pressure was 16 mm Hg in both eyes. | 5. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye revealed a normal optic disc, mild venous engorgement, and widespread peripheral dot-blot retinal hemorrhages mainly located in the temporal midperiphery (Figure 1A). | 6. No spontaneous retinal arterial pulsation was noted. | 8. Fluorescein angiography in the right eye showed delayed venous filling, mild perifoveal leakage, and scattered microaneurysms in the temporal sector (Figure 1B). | 9. A, Montage color fundus photograph of the right eye at presentation shows mild venous dilation and midperipheral dot and blot hemorrhages mostly located in the temporal sectors. | 10. B, Fluorescein angiography frame (2 minutes, 3 seconds) shows multiple microaneurysms in correspondence of the dot-blot retinal hemorrhages and a barely visible perifoveal vascular leakage.

1. A woman in her mid-20s presented with subacute bilateral vision loss that was worse in the left eye. | 2. Her medical history was remarkable for type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 16 years of age and proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes that had been treated with panretinal photocoagulation 7 years earlier. | 3. She had undergone pars plana vitrectomy with endolaser to treat a tractional retinal detachment in her right eye 2 years before this presentation. | 4. She also had a history of hypertension and chronic kidney disease, and she was 15 weeks into pregnancy. | 5. Visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/100 OS. | 8. The patient was in no apparent distress and denied any headache, chest pain, or focal weakness. | 9. Ophthalmoscopic examination (Figure) revealed mild optic nerve head edema that was greater in the left eye than the right eye with associated nerve fiber layer hemorrhage in the left eye. | 10. Nerve fiber layer infarctions, dot and blot hemorrhages, and lesions caused by panretinal photocoagulation also were seen bilaterally. | 11. Optical coherence tomography showed macular edema that involved the center of the macula in both eyes (Figure, inset).

1. A woman in her 50s presented to our emergency department with a 3-hour history of sudden epigastric and right upper quadrant pain. | 2. She did not report any previous abdominal surgery. | 3. The colicky pain did not migrate during that period and occurred in paroxysms at 9- to 10-minute intervals. | 4. The patient was afebrile and had no nausea or vomiting. | 5. Physical examination revealed mild tachycardia (96/min) and moderate abdominal distension without signs of peritonism; the bowel sounds were hyperactive. | 6. Careful examination ruled out incarcerated hernias in the groin, femoral triangle, and obturator foramen. | 7. Blood analysis results showed mild leukocytosis (total white blood cell count, 10.5 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109 per liter, multiply by 0.001]) without elevation of the C-reactive protein level (<3 mg/L [to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 9.524]). | 8. Serum electrolyte levels were within the normal range. | 12. Arrowheads indicate the border of the epiploic foramen; asterisk, the air-filled cecum in the lesser sac.Lesser sac (omental bursa) internal hernia through the epiploic foramen

1. A 57-year-old woman with non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and no other medical history had worsening left-sided back pain over 4 months and no other symptoms. | 2. Physical examination findings were significant for mild left flank pain, but there was no costovertebral angle tenderness. | 3. Laboratory results were within normal limits. | 4. Axial imaging demonstrated an exophytic, retroperitoneal mass with solid and cystic components involving the left kidney, posterior abdominal wall, and mesocolon (Figure 1). | 5. The mass measured 20 cm in its greatest dimension. | 6. Findings on colonoscopy and mammography were negative. | 7. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography did not reveal any other abnormality.Coronal computed tomographic image showing a retroperitoneal mass with a cystic component and involvement of adjacent kidney and mesocolon. | 8. Red arrowhead indicates descending colon; blue arrowhead, left kidney invaded by mass; and yellow arrowhead, retroperitoneal mass with cystic component.

1. A 54-year-old White woman with a history of lobular breast carcinoma in situ treated with lumpectomy as well as chromophobe kidney cell carcinoma treated with partial nephrectomy was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic, amelanotic choroidal mass in her left eye, suspicious for metastatic disease. | 2. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU and intraocular pressures were normal in both eyes at 10 mm Hg. | 3. Slitlamp biomicroscopy of the anterior chamber was within normal limits in both eyes. | 4. Dilated fundus examination revealed normal findings in the right eye and clear vitreous with a subretinal mass in the left eye inferior to the optic disc and measuring 3 × 2 mm in base. | 5.
