1. A 4-week-old boy presents to the pediatrician for vomiting. | 2. The patient is breastfed and typically feeds for 20-30 minutes every 2 hours. | 3. One week ago, he began vomiting and regurgitating breastmilk through his nose after most feedings. | 4. His stools over the past week have also become blood-streaked. | 5. The patient does not seem to be in any distress when he passes these bloody stools. | 6. The patient surpassed his birth weight by 2 weeks of age but has fallen 1 standard deviation on the growth curve since then. | 7. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 78/47 mmHg, pulse is 115/min, and respirations are 28/min. | 8. On physical exam, the patient is well-appearing. | 10. The patient’s abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. | 11. A digital rectal exam reveals a small amount of blood in the rectal vault.

1. A 74-year-old man with a history of multiple squamous cell carcinomas that were treated with Mohs micrographic surgery presented with a tender, enlarging scalp lesion of 6 months’ duration. | 2. Skin examination revealed a 5-mm bright pink, dome-shaped papule with overlying vessels located at the crown of the scalp (Figure, A). | 3. C, Proliferation of tumor cells is present around small vessels with scattered mitoses (black arrowhead) and necrosis (yellow arrowheads) (hematoxylin-eosin).

1. A woman in her 60s presented with numerous whitish papules on the back of more than 10 years’ duration. | 2. The lesions previously resolved with topical corticosteroids but flared soon after treatment discontinuation. | 3. Some papules became pruritic and extended to the waist and anterior trunk in the past month. | 5. Physical examination revealed multiple hypopigmented, flat-topped papules on the back, waist, and inframammary area without genital involvement (Figure, A). | 6. Most lesions were folliculocentric under close inspection. | 7. Dermoscopy revealed central keratin plugs and some foci of structureless, whitish, and homogenous areas with surrounding erythema (Figure, B). | 8. The results of laboratory tests for antinuclear antibody and hyperglobulinemia were negative. | 10. A, Multiple hypopigmented, atrophic, keratotic, and folliculocentric papules are seen on the trunk. | 11. B, Dermascopic findings included 2 foci of central keratin plugs and another ill-defined, whitish, and homogenous area with surrounding erythema.

1. A 34-year-old man presented with headache, double vision, and seizures for 1 month and altered consciousness for 1 week. | 2. He had had 2 episodes of seizures that were characterized by tonic head and eye deviation to the left, followed by a brief period of tonic-clonic activity of all 4 limbs and postictal confusion for 10 to 15 minutes. | 3. He denied a history of fever, head trauma, limb weakness, or vomiting. | 6. On examination, he was confused. | 7. He had facial flushing and grade III clubbing in his fingers and toes. | 8. His chest and cardiovascular examination results were normal. | 9. He had ptosis in his right eye. | 10. The right eye was deviated laterally secondary to right-medial rectus palsy. | 11. His pupil size and pupillary light reactions were normal. | 12. He also had grade II papilledema. | 13. His motor and sensory examination results were normal; however, he had brisk deep-tendon jerks and extensor planter responses. | 14. There were no meningeal signs. | 15. His cranial magnetic resonance image showed 2 ring-enhancing lesions in the right frontal and left parietal cortexes, along with surrounding brain edema and mass effects. | 16. Both lesions showed a thin-walled, contrast-enhancing rim with a central liquefaction (Figure, A). | 17. The central liquefaction showed restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance images. | 18. A, Cranial T1-weighted postcontrast magnetic resonance image showing ring-enhancing lesions in the right frontal and left parietal lobes. | 19. B, Chest radiography showing a radiolucent nodular shadow in left middle lung field. | 20. His hemoglobin level was 19.3 grams per deciliter (to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10.0), his total leukocyte count was 13 500/μL (to convert to cells × 10^9/L, multiply by 0.001), his hematocrit was 62.4% (to convert to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 10), and his platelet count was 210 000/μL (to convert to cells × 10^9/L, multiply by 0.001).

1. An 8-month-old white male was seen for evaluation of a red, bleeding umbilical mass. | 2. The lesion had been present since loss of the umbilical stump at 1 week of life. | 3. It bled easily with Valsalva maneuver or trauma. | 4. The lesion was treated as an infantile hemangioma with timolol by an outside dermatologist and as an umbilical pyogenic granuloma with silver nitrate by the patient’s pediatrician, with minimal improvement. | 5. The patient was born at 38½ weeks by normal spontaneous vaginal delivery. | 7. On examination, he was an alert and healthy-appearing child. | 8. The umbilicus demonstrated a bright red, friable, 5-mm papule (Figure, A). | 9. A shave biopsy specimen was obtained for histologic examination (Figure, B and C).A, Clinical photograph of the red friable papule in the umbilicus. | 10. B and C, Hematoxylin-eosin–stained shave biopsy specimen showing an ulcerated epidermis, colonic mucosa, and granulation tissue (B, original magnification ×2.7; C, original magnification ×10).

1. A 78-year-old man with a history of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism who had been taking warfarin for the last 20 years presented with 1 day of severe abdominal pain, which began after eating dinner. | 3. On examination, he was afebrile and had a normal heart rate but was notably hypotensive. | 4. He was given 2 L of crystalloid, and his blood pressure responded appropriately. | 5. His physical examination showed an abdomen that was soft but diffusely tender without rebound or guarding. | 7. Blood testing revealed an elevated creatinine level of 1.7 mg/dL (to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 88.4), an elevated lactate level of 29.7 mg/dL (to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 0.111), an international normalized ratio of 4.6, a lowered hemoglobin level of 10.7 g/dL (to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10), and a lowered hematocrit level of 27.2%; all other results were unremarkable. | 8. Given his coagulopathy, low hematocrit level, and abdominal pain, a computed tomography angiogram was performed to rule out bleeding (Figure 1).A, Axial cross-section computed tomography without contrast of the abdomen and pelvis revealed gallstones in the neck of the gallbladder, high-density material within the lumen, and free intraperitoneal fluid. | 9. B, Axial cross-section computed tomography with intravenous contrast was significant for a blush of contrast within the lumen of the gallbladder and surrounding hyperemia of the liver at the gallbladder fossa.Hemorrhagic shock secondary to perforated hemorrhagic calculous cholecystitis

1. A girl in her teens with a history of postconcussion syndrome was referred for retinal evaluation after failing her vision examination for her learner's permit for driving. | 2. She complained of progressively declining, blurred vision for 2 years. | 3. She denied floaters, flashes of light, headaches, and eye pain. | 4. The patient had a concussion 1 year prior after becoming dehydrated during marching band practice, fainting, and hitting her head on pavement. | 5. Her postconcussion symptoms included headaches, dizziness, and dysarthria. | 6. The headaches and dizziness resolved but the dysarthria remained. | 7. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within the last year was normal. | 8. She denied acute vision changes after the concussion. | 9. Family history was unremarkable for vision loss, glaucoma, inherited retinal degeneration, and autoimmune disease.Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OU. | 10. Ishihara testing revealed red-green color deficiency bilaterally. | 11. Intraocular pressures, extraocular motility, confrontational visual fields, and pupils were normal. | 12. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable. | 13. Ophthalmoscopic examination demonstrated mild mottled retinal pigment epithelial abnormalities bilaterally (Figure, A).Right eye multicolor fundus image and retinal spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT). | 14. A, Multicolor fundus image demonstrates mild macular mottling. | 15. The optic disc and retinal vessels are unremarkable. | 16. B, Retinal SD-OCT shows normal foveal contour with disruption and loss of the interdigitation and ellipsoid zones subfoveally.Fundus autofluorescence showed bilateral mild macular hyperautofluorescence likely within normal range without evidence of flecks. | 17. Retinal spectral-domain optical coherence tomography demonstrated bilateral disruption of the interdigitation and ellipsoid zones subfoveally (Figure, B). | 18. Electroretinogram (ERG) revealed delayed and decreased amplitude responses to 30-Hz flicker with normal dark-adapted responses. | 19. Goldmann visual field testing showed mild bilateral nasal constriction.Two months after presentation, the patient returned with new balance difficulties and worsening dysarthria. | 20. Horizontal and vertical saccades were markedly slowed bilaterally.

1. An elderly man presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of new-onset, persistent lower abdominal and flank pain. | 2. The pain was sharp and constant with intermittent radiation to the back and associated anorexia with a 10-kg weight loss. | 5. Physical examination revealed he was afebrile and in normal sinus rhythm; there was minimal epigastric abdominal tenderness without signs of peritonitis and no palpable masses. | 6. Femoral pulses were palpable and symmetric. | 7. Laboratory examination revealed mild anemia (hematocrit, 35% [to convert to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01]), no leukocytosis, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (71 mm/h). | 8. Blood and urine cultures were negative for organisms. | 9. A computed tomographic (CT) angiogram showed asymmetric attenuation surrounding the infrarenal aorta (Figure 1). | 10. On comparison, a CT scan that was performed 6 months before presentation had identified no aneurysmal disease.Computed tomographic scan with arterial phase intravenous contrast with asymmetric attenuation surrounding the infrarenal aorta.

1. A woman in her late 60s presented with progressive, painless blurring of vision in both eyes over the past 6 months. | 2. Medical history was significant for Sjögren syndrome, for which she was taking hydroxychloroquine sulfate. | 3. Ocular history was notable for neovascular age-related macular degeneration under good control with intravitreal injections in the right eye and intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration in the left eye. | 4. Family history was negative for corneal disease. | 5. On initial presentation to the clinic, the best-corrected visual acuity of the patient was 20/150 OD and 20/40 OS. | 6. She was found to have bilateral, gray-white, irregular, poorly circumscribed, linear and nummular central and peripheral corneal opacities, confined primarily to the subepithelium and focally to the underlying anterior stroma (Figure 1A). | 7. The epithelium itself and deeper corneal stroma were spared, and the remainder of her anterior segment and fundus examination results were within normal limits. | 8. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography documented deposition of hyperreflective material in the subepithelium with trace deposition in the anterior stroma (Figure 1B). | 10. A, Right eye gray-white, irregular, linear and nummular central and peripheral corneal opacities. | 11. The left eye had similar findings. | 12. B, Hyperreflective deposits in the subepithelium (black arrowhead) with trace deposit in the anterior stroma (white arrowhead).

1. A 69-year-old woman presents with pain in her hip and groin. | 2. The pain is present in the morning but is nearly unbearable by the end of the day. | 3. Her medical history is notable for a treated episode of acute renal failure, diabetes mellitus, obesity, and hypertension. | 5. The patient recently started taking high doses of vitamin D as she believes that it could help her symptoms. | 6. She also recently fell off the treadmill while exercising at the gym. | 7. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 135/91 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 12/min. | 8. On exam, an obese woman in no distress is noted. | 9. There is pain, decreased range of motion, and crepitus on exam of her right hip. | 10. The patient points to the areas that cause her pain stating that it is mostly over the groin.

1. A 2-day-old girl (weight, 3.7 kg) developed abdominal distention and vomiting after feeding. | 2. Her Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes were 7 and 9, respectively. | 3. The infant’s postnatal course was remarkable for a febrile episode that was presumed to be due to chorioamnionitis in the mother and for which antibiotic treatment was initiated. | 4. Findings from the prenatal ultrasound, most recently conducted at 33 weeks’ gestation, were normal. | 5. The infant was active and well perfused, with a soft but distended abdomen and right-sided labial swelling. | 6. Findings from the remainder of her examination were unremarkable. | 7. An abdominal radiograph revealed dilated small-bowel loops (Figure 1A). | 8. Radiography of the upper gastrointestinal tract with water-soluble contrast showed a normal pattern of rotation. | 9. Results of a suction rectal biopsy revealed ganglion cells to be present. | 12. B, Delayed radiography of the upper gastrointestinal tract with water-soluble contrast demonstrating retained contrast in the terminal ileum 6 days after initial radiography.

1. A woman in her 50s admitted for bacterial pneumonia was noted to have an ulcerated plaque on the forearm. | 2. The patient had been discharged approximately 2 weeks prior, after an admission for congestive heart failure. | 3. A few days after that discharge, the patient noticed a painful ulceration on the right distal forearm, at the site where a peripheral intravenous catheter had been inserted during her initial hospitalization. | 4. On physical examination, the patient had an ulcerated plaque on the right forearm with 2 tender, 1- to 2-cm red nodules in the right antecubital fossa (Figure, A). | 5. On further questioning, the patient noted that between her hospitalizations she had gone home and cleaned her fish tank, played with her pet cat, and gardened in her indoor cactus garden. | 7. A skin biopsy and culture were performed from the forearm lesion (Figure, B and C). | 8. A, An ulcerated plaque on the right forearm. | 9. Note 2 tender, 1- to 2-cm red nodules in the right antecubital fossa. | 10. B, Dense neutrophilic infiltrate. | 11. Note associated tissue necrosis. | 12. Hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×20. | 13. C, Organisms seen on Gram stain.

1. A man in his 60s presented to our clinic with a 5-year history of diffuse erythematous, edematous annular plaques (Figure 1); low-grade fevers; and mild leukopenia. | 2. The result of a skin biopsy performed 4 years prior was interpreted as subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE). | 3. Treatments included hydroxychloroquine, 400 mg/d, for 4 years; mycophenolate mofetil, 1000 mg/d, for 6 months; and oral prednisone tapers, starting at 40 mg/d. | 4. Of these, only prednisone appeared to elicit a response. | 5. Review of symptoms was negative for fatigue, weight loss, cough, shortness of breath, joint pain, ocular symptoms, mucosal ulcerations, history of blood clots, photosensitivity, pleurisy, urine changes, and diarrhea. | 6. Medical history included hypertension, for which he took losartan, and seasonal allergies, for which he used fexofenadine and fluticasone. | 7. Laboratory evaluation revealed mild neutropenia and lymphopenia with normal hemoglobin and platelet counts. | 8. Antinuclear antibody screening results were negative. | 9. The results of a comprehensive metabolic panel, C3, C4, serum protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine, ferritin, copper, zinc, haptoglobin, HIV, hepatitis B and C serologic tests, and rapid plasma reagin were negative. | 10. Lactate dehydrogenase was mildly elevated. | 11. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 41 mm/h. | 13. Therapeutic trials of dapsone and dapsone in combination with colchicine were not effective.

1. A woman in her 80s presented with a 1-year history of blanchable, salmon-colored, monomorphic macules and fine telangiectasias localized to her right lower leg (Figure, A). | 2. The asymptomatic patch had slowly enlarged since initial onset, but remained confined to the single extremity. | 3. Physical examination revealed agminated and discrete erythematous macules as well as interspersed fine, reticulated telangiectases over the right pretibial leg (Figure, B). | 4. No edema or warmth of the affected area was observed, and there was no evidence of mucosal, conjunctival, or nail involvement. | 5. Findings on review of systems were negative for bleeding tendencies or hypercoagulability. | 6. A punch biopsy was performed (Figure, C and D). | 7. A, Reticulated, blanchable, salmon-colored patch on the pretibial leg. | 8. B, Individual fine, telangiectatic erythematous macules identified on closer inspection. | 9. C, Concentric deposits of hyaline material surround dilated and markedly thickened capillaries within the papillary dermis (original magnification ×200). | 10. D, Perivascular hyaline deposits are highlighted strongly by periodic acid–Schiff stain (original magnification ×200).

1. A 16-year-old girl presents with acute left shoulder pain, left-sided chest pain, and shortness of breath, with a history of intermittent left shoulder and left-sided chest pain for 4 months following a dance recital. | 2. She has been treated with analgesia and physiotherapy. | 3. She denies fever, cough, orthopnea, weight loss, and appetite change. | 4. Physical examination reveals tenderness at the location of the left fifth rib and reduced left chest expansion. | 5. There is no chest wall deformity. | 6. Chest radiography (Figure 1) shows left lower lobe opacification obscuring the left hemidiaphragm and blunting of the left costophrenic angle.Left, Anteroposterior chest radiograph.

1. A healthy woman in her 60s presented with multiple erythematous crusted plaques on her trunk that had appeared 4 weeks previously, sparing her limbs and facial region (Figure, A). | 2. She had a long-standing history of several outbreaks of skin lesions limited to both axillae and groin. | 3. Previous episodes had been successfully treated with various topical drugs that were administered by her primary care physician. | 4. No family history of similar lesions was recorded. | 5. Physical examination revealed multiple annular erythematous plaques surrounded by a peripheral crusted and pustular collarette on her trunk (Figure, B). | 6. No active lesions were present in her axillae, inframammary folds, or groin. | 7. After obtaining informed consent, 2 biopsy specimens were taken from the periphery of the lesion for hematoxylin-eosin stain and direct immunofluorescence (Figure, C and D). | 8. A skin swab specimen from a pustular lesion was taken for microbiological culture.A, Multiple erythematous and crusted plaques diffusely distributed on the dorsal trunk at presentation. | 9. B, An erythematous annular plaque, surrounded by a crusted and focally pustular peripheral collarette. | 10. C and D, Histopathologic images, hematoxylin-eosin. | 11. C, Biopsy specimen revealing suprabasilar acantholysis (original magnification ×4). | 12. D, Specimen from generalized lesions at clinical presentation (original magnification ×40).

1. A 64-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive bilateral proptosis and conjunctival erythema. | 2. Her medical history was significant for hypothyroidism, treated with levothyroxine, as well as 2 forms of hematologic malignancy: retroperitoneal extranodal marginal zone lymphoma and indolent-phase T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia. | 3. She had received no treatment for her hematologic malignancies, as she had been asymptomatic since her diagnoses 6 years prior. | 4. Ophthalmological examination revealed 27 mm of bilateral proptosis, conjunctival injection, chemosis, and bilateral lower eyelid retraction (Figure 1A). | 6. Extraocular motility was full in all positions of gaze, and there was no associated pain. | 8. Von Graefe sign (delayed descent of the upper eyelid with initiation of downgaze) and lagophthalmos were absent. | 9. Results of slitlamp examination and dilated fundus examination were normal, including the appearance of both optic nerves. | 11. There is mild temporal retraction of both upper eyelids. | 12. B, Radiographic images documenting marked enlargement of all extraocular muscles bilaterally. | 13. The lateral rectus is especially enlarged on both sides. | 14. Using a measurement technique described by Dagi and colleagues, the maximal diameter of each extraocular muscle in this patient was as follows: right inferior rectus, 8.0 mm; right medial rectus, 9.1 mm; right superior muscle group, 9.7 mm; right lateral rectus, 9.3 mm; left inferior rectus, 8.1 mm; left medial rectus, 9.5 mm; left superior muscle group, 10.0 mm; and left lateral rectus, 9.6 mm. | 15. There is sparing of anterior tendinous insertions (arrowheads) of each medial rectus (MR) and lateral rectus (LR). | 16. However, the anterior portion of the muscle belly (brackets) appears uninvolved compared with the posterior portion, causing an acute taper of the muscle that is similar in shape to an amphora (inset). | 17. An orbital computed tomography scan revealed marked enlargement of all extraocular muscles (Figure 1B). | 18. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin, and thyroid peroxidase antibody levels were normal.

1. A female patient in her late 40s presented with a 3-year history of nonhealing ulcers in her groin and axillae. | 2. These lesions started as itchy, weepy, reddish papules and plaques, which gradually progressed to form ulcers and were associated with pain and pus discharge. | 3. They did not heal completely after multiple courses of topical as well as systemic antibiotics, antifungals, and steroids. | 4. She frequently experienced scaling and greasiness on her scalp, which was treated with shampoos and topical steroids. | 5. She also complained of polyuria and polydipsia for the past 4 years. | 6. General examination revealed multiple mobile, firm, nonmatted, and nontender lymph nodes in cervical and inguinal region. | 7. On systemic examination, hepatomegaly (2 cm below the right costal margin) was seen. | 8. There was also bilateral enlargement of the parotid area, which was tender on palpation. | 9. Cutaneous examination revealed yellowish greasy scales on the scalp, suggestive of seborrheic dermatitis. | 10. Erythematous edematous papules were present over the retroauricular areas and the inframammary folds (Figure, A). | 11. On examination of external genitalia, deep ulcers were observed in the bilateral inguinal folds, resembling knife-cut ulcers (Figure, B). | 12. Similar lesions were present over the junction of labia majora and labia minora and were associated with yellowish pus discharge. | 13. A 3.5-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathological examination from the edge of an ulcer on one of the groin folds (Figure, C and D). | 15. B, Deep ulcers in the groin folds resembling knife-cut ulcers with yellowish pus discharge. | 16. C, Histopathological examination of the area with intact epidermis shows dense infiltration of the ulcer bed by atypical cells. | 17. These cells were large and had characteristic grooved vesicular nuclei and moderate amphophilic cytoplasm. | 18. D, Immunohistochemistry shows diffuse positivity for CD1a in the lower epidermis and dermis.

1. A man in his late 60s with a history of laryngeal cancer was transferred to our institution. | 2. The patient had undergone laryngectomy with radiation, modified radical neck dissection, and a pectoralis major flap into the right-sided neck wound in 1998. | 3. This operation was subsequently complicated by right carotid blowout requiring right-sided carotid artery ligation on November 5, 2005. | 4. The patient initially presented to our hospital with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3. | 5. Findings from computed tomography of the head at the referring hospital showed acute right-hemispheric stroke with left-sided hemiparesis. | 6. On examination, the patient was afebrile, with a heart rate of 108 beats/min and blood pressure of 169/91 mm Hg with 100% oxygen saturation. | 7. Pertinent findings included an improved Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12 and left arm and leg hemiparesis. | 8. The right upper arm was cool to the touch below the elbow, with cyanotic right fingers, and the right-sided radial and brachial pulses were absent. | 9. The patient also presented with a pulsatile mass in the upper chest wall on the right side.

1. A man in his 30s with AIDS presented with acute-onset painful scattered umbilicated papulopustules and ovoid ulcerated plaques with elevated, pink borders on the face, trunk, and extremities (Figure, A). | 2. The patient also had a new-onset cough but was afebrile and denied other systemic symptoms. | 3. Due to his significant immunocompromise, the clinical presentation was highly suspicious for infection. | 4. For rapid bedside differentiation of multiple infectious etiologies, a Tzanck smear was performed by scraping the base of an ulcerated lesion and inner aspect of a pseudopustule and scraping its base with a #15 blade. | 5. These contents were placed on a glass slide, fixed, and stained with Wright-Giemsa and subsequently Papanicolaou staining to further characterize the changes seen.A, Clinical image demonstrating papulopustules and ovoid ulcerated plaques with elevated, pink borders on the elbows. | 6. B, Tzanck smear using Wright-Giemsa staining of specimen demonstrating ballooning of keratinocytes and peripheralization of nuclear material (original magnification ×20).

1. A 74-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of retinal lesions in her left eye. | 2. Her ocular history was notable for recent cataract surgery 5 weeks prior to presentation that was complicated by endophthalmitis. | 3. A normal funduscopic examination was documented prior to cataract surgery. | 4. At the time of initial presentation to her local retina specialist 1 week following her cataract surgery, the patient had severe pain and redness. | 5. Her visual acuity was light perception. | 6. An examination revealed a 2-mm hypopyon and dense vitreous haze with no view of the retina. | 7. She was treated for presumed endophthalmitis with a vitreous tap and intravitreal injections of vancomycin (1 mg/0.1 mL), ceftazidime (2.2 mg/0.1 mL), and dexamethasone (0.4 mg/0.1 mL). | 8. The vitreous sample obtained at the time of treatment grew Staphylococcus caprae susceptible to vancomycin. | 9. At time of examination in our clinic 4 weeks following treatment, the patient was receiving topical steroid and cycloplegic drops. | 10. Her best-corrected visual acuity had improved to 20/70. | 11. Examination showed a deep and quiet anterior chamber with a well-positioned intraocular lens without any plaques or deposits on the lens capsule. | 12. Dilated ophthalmoscopic examination demonstrated improvement in the vitreous debris with 1+ vitritis and numerous superficial, round, white lesions spread throughout the fundus in all 4 quadrants and in the macula (Figure 1A). | 14. A, Fundus photograph of the left eye at presentation shows vitreous debris with numerous white lesions throughout the retina. | 15. B, Optical coherence tomography demonstrates discrete preretinal hyperreflective lesions.

1. A white woman in her 50s without significant medical history underwent breast augmentation surgery with saline implants without postoperative complications. | 2. Five years later, she underwent a bilateral augmentation mammoplasty with removal and replacement of silicone gel implants and major mastopexy with capsulotomy. | 3. Although the patient’s surgical course was uncomplicated, several months postoperatively she noted persistent asymptomatic rough areas that she assumed were scars. | 5. On physical examination, the patient had well-healed, barely identifiable scars on the inframammary creases and lower breast areas. | 6. Separate from the scars and located on the inferior medial bilateral breasts were 1- to 2-cm slightly erythematous annular atrophic plaques with more involvement of the left breast than the right. | 7. The rims of the lesions were raised with slight white scale and the centers slightly depressed and wrinkled in appearance (Figure 1). | 8. Clinical images of the inferior medial bilateral breasts with 1- to 2-cm erythematous annular atrophic plaques with more involvement of the left breast (A) than the right (B).

1. A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room by his mother, who states that her son has been coughing uncontrollably for 3 hours. | 2. The child has a medical history of obesity and atopic dermatitis and uses topical steroid cream. | 5. His temperature is 98.5°F (36.9°C), pulse is 120/min, blood pressure is 90/52 mmHg, and respirations are 32/min. | 6. On exam, he appears uncomfortable, is coughing continuously, and is drooling.

1. A woman in her early 80s with a history of systemic hypertension and heart failure presented with retinal changes in both eyes. | 3. The patient had no visual complaints but stated that it was difficult for her to see at night. | 5. Visual acuity was 20/50 OU and pupillary responses, external examination, extraocular motility, and intraocular pressures were normal. | 6. Confrontation visual field testing showed peripheral constriction in each eye. | 7. Slitlamp examination showed the absence of anterior chamber inflammation and the presence of posterior chamber intraocular lenses and liquefied vitreous with a few vitreous strands bilaterally. | 8. Fundus examination (Figure, A) revealed poor foveal light reflexes, an annular pattern of outer retinal hypopigmentation approximating the border of the temporal arcades, and inferotemporal clumped pigment deposits in each eye. | 9. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (Figure, B) showed outer retinal foveoschisis as well as outer retinal thinning with interruptions in the ellipsoid in the peripheral macula in each eye. | 10. Fluorescein angiography showed no disc leakage or angiographic macular edema (Figure, C); there was faint staining of the annular area of hypopigmentation seen on fundus examination. | 11. Fundus autofluorescence showed a ring of abnormal hyperautofluorescence.A, Fundus photograph of the right eye shows poor foveal light reflex, an annular pattern of outer retinal hypopigmentation approximating the border of the temporal arcade, and inferotemporal clumped pigment deposits (seen in both eyes). | 12. B, Spectral-domain optical coherence tomographic (SD-OCT) image of the right eye shows outer retinal foveoschisis and outer retinal thinning with interruptions of the ellipsoid in the peripheral macula (seen in both eyes). | 13. C, Fluorescein angiogram at 1 minute 15 seconds in the right eye shows no disc leakage or angiographic macular edema; there is faint staining of the annular area of hypopigmentation seen on the fundus photograph.

1. A woman in her mid-70s with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, end-stage renal disease, and coronary artery disease was admitted to the hospital for fever, lethargy, and altered mental status. | 2. On day 7 of her hospital stay, she developed severe, unremitting left ankle pain with purpuric lesions on the skin. | 3. She had previously undergone coronary artery bypass grafting with simultaneous aortic valve replacement and ileal conduit urinary diversion as a result of to recurrent upper urinary tract infections. | 4. Laboratory findings were significant for neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis (leukocyte count, 19 400/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]). | 5. Physical examination revealed multiple stellate, purpuric plaques with central flaccid bullae on the medial and lateral aspects of the left ankle (Figure, A). | 6. The remainder of her skin examination findings were unremarkable. | 8. A, Stellate purpura with overlying flaccid bulla on the medial aspect of the ankle. | 9. B, Partially necrotic epidermis with intraepidermal bulla formation with marked perivascular infiltrates in the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×25).

1. A 6-week-old girl presents with her parents to the pediatrician for blood-streaked diapers. | 2. The patient is breastfed every 2-3 hours and voids 10-12 times daily. | 3. The patient previously had several soft stools per day that ranged in color from mustard yellow to dark green. | 4. Over the past 2 days, the patient’s stools have become looser and streaked with blood. | 5. The patient has also regurgitated several of her feedings in the last few days. | 6. Neither the vomit nor bloody stools have seemed to bother the patient. | 7. The patient’s weight continues to trend along the 50th percentile. | 8. The patient’s temperature is 98.4°F (36.9°C), blood pressure is 66/51 mmHg, pulse is 127/min, and respirations are 26/min. | 9. On physical exam, the patient appears well nourished and is cooing. | 10. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender.

1. A 59-year-old man presented to the vitreoretinal service with a 2-week history of acute-onset, progressively worsening decreased vision and central scotomas in both eyes. | 2. He had no systemic symptoms and denied having eye redness, pain, and photophobia. | 3. His medical and surgical history included prostate cancer, status postcryotherapy, osteoarthritis, and migraines. | 4. His social history was significant for active cigarette smoking and immigration from a Middle Eastern country. | 5. His medications included naproxen at 500 mg as needed, tamsulosin at 0.4 mg daily, and aspirin at 81 mg daily. | 6. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuities were 20/40 OD and 20/25 OS. | 7. His pupils were reactive, his extraocular motility was full, and the intraocular pressures were 16 mm Hg in both eyes. | 8. The results of the external examination and anterior slitlamp examinations were unremarkable, and there was no anterior chamber or anterior vitreous cell or flare. | 9. The dilated fundus photography examination revealed yellow-gray, curvilinear, and puzzle piece–shaped subretinal macular lesions in both eyes (Figure). | 10. The lesions were hyperfluorescent with hypofluorescent borders on fundus autofluorescence testing results (Figure). | 11. Optical coherence tomography revealed that the involved areas exhibited a disruption of the outer retinal layers (including and deep to the outer nuclear layer) along with hyperreflectivity of the outer retina, retinal pigment epithelium, and choroid. | 12. There was no involvement of the inner retina. | 13. The patient underwent laboratory testing for syphilis and tuberculosis, which yielded negative results. | 14. Fundus photographs showing yellowish, puzzle piece–shaped, curvilinear lesions in the maculae of the right eye (A) and left eye (B).

1. A 70-year-old man presented to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of a pruritic exanthem that began on his scalp and face and spread across most of his body over a 2-month period. | 2. The patient had no fever, night sweats, fatigue, recent unintentional weight loss, shortness of breath, chest pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. | 3. He reported no new prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements prior to the onset of the exanthem. | 5. On presentation, his temperature was 37.1 °C (98.7 °F); blood pressure, 128/86 mm Hg; heart rate, 110/min; and respiratory rate, 30/min. | 6. Physical examination revealed confluent salmon-colored plaques composed of folliculocentric scaly papules across his body with several patches of unaffected skin on his trunk. | 7. The patient had waxy, exfoliative scale on the volar aspect of his hands and feet and thickened, onycholytic nails. | 8. Severe ectropion prevented complete eyelid closure (Figure). | 9. He was referred to the emergency department, where laboratory testing revealed a normal complete blood cell count and normal lactate dehydrogenase level. | 10. The patient was admitted to the hospital and was treated with intravenous fluids and daily wet-wrap therapy with topical triamcinolone ointment (0.1%) applied to his trunk, arms, and legs, followed by a layer of warm, damp gauze and dry, cotton pajamas. | 11. Clinical examination at the time of presentation revealed generalized and coalescing salmon-colored plaques with “islands of sparing” on the abdomen (far left); waxy, exfoliative scale on the palms (center left) and soles (center right); and ectropion (far right).

1. A woman in her 30s presented for evaluation of asymptomatic erythematous scaly plaques over the face and proximal extremities. | 2. The lesions started as an erythematous papule on the face, which had progressed to larger plaques within 10 years. | 3. There was involvement of the upper respiratory tract, causing palatal perforation and stridor, necessitating a tracheostomy a year ago. | 4. Examination revealed multiple well-defined brown erythematous scaly plaques with central scarring measuring 2 × 1 to 8 × 7 cm on the face, arm, and thighs. | 7. The patient also had saddle nose deformity, perforation of the hard palate, and necrotic plaques on the ear, causing destruction of ear cartilage (Figure, A and B). | 8. There was cervical lymphadenopathy: multiple, nontender, discrete nodes, ranging from 1.5 to 2 cm without any surface changes. | 10. Respiratory examination and chest radiography results were normal. | 11. Hemogram showed anemia (hemoglobin, 10.1 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0]); the results of a kidney function test, a liver function test, a fasting blood glucose test, and routine urinalysis were within normal limits. | 12. Serologic analysis results for HIV-1/2, antinuclear antibody, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. | 13. Punch skin biopsy was obtained for histopathologic analysis and culture (Figure, C). | 14. A, Multiple well-defined brown erythematous scaly plaques with central scarring, saddle nose deformity, and necrotic lesions on the ear with loss of ear cartilage. | 15. B, Perforation of the hard palate. | 16. C, Infiltrate of foamy histiocytes and pigmented yeasts without multiaxial septation (Fontana-Masson).

1. A 53-year-old man received a diagnosis of stage IV melanoma with metastatic disease to the spine and brain 3 months before presentation. | 2. Four weeks following receipt of immunotherapy with ipilimumab and nivolumab, he developed acute abdominal pain in the setting of a rapidly rising lactic acid dehydrogenase levels, prompting hospital admission. | 3. Imaging results showed mild disease progression (new ascites and periportal metabolic lymph node). | 4. Splenic infarct and portal/splenic vein thrombi were identified as etiologies of his acute pain and were presumed to be secondary to hypercoagulable state of malignancy. | 5. Over the next 3 days, he had rising serum creatinine (sCr) levels (baseline, approximately 1 mg/dL [to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4]). | 7. Ultrasonography results showed abnormal intraparenchymal flow to both kidneys without evidence of kidney artery stenosis. | 8. Urine studies were consistent with prerenal etiology, while the presence of casts suggested acute tubular necrosis. | 9. Nephrotoxic medications (omeprazole/pantoprazole) were discontinued. | 10. The top differential diagnoses at this juncture included contrast-induced nephropathy or immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)–induced acute interstitial nephritis, and empirical high dose steroids were prescribed. | 11. Despite observation and steroid treatment, his sCr levels continued to increase over the next 5 days, peaking at 5.8 mg/dL, and the patient progressed into anuric kidney failure, requiring hemodialysis. | 12. This prompted a kidney biopsy for definitive diagnosis (Figure). | 13. One week later, he received encorafenib, a BRAF inhibitor. | 14. Two weeks later, the patient’s kidney function began to improve, and hemodialysis was discontinued. | 15. He continued to show gradual improvement, with a return to near baseline kidney function (sCr level, 1.3 mg/dL) approximately 6 weeks after treatment initiation. | 16. Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).

B, Enlarged fundus photograph shows nummular macular lesions with mild retina striae and optic disc edema.

Slitlamp photograph of the anterior segment (A) and optical coherence tomographic imaging of the lens–capsular bag complex (B) obtained at initial presentation (arrowheads show hyperdistention of the capsular bag with turbid fluid).

1. A 55-year old woman presented with a 6-week history of an enlarging, tender, pruritic, 4-cm erythematous patch with central inflammatory papules distributed on the medial forehead (Figure, A). | 3. 1. An 8-year-old boy presented to the pediatric emergency department with 2 weeks of fatigue and 3 days of double vision, ptosis, and painless periorbital swelling of the left eye. | 4. The right pupil was 3.5 mm and briskly reactive, while the left pupil was 8.5 mm and unreactive to light or near effort; there was no relative afferent pupillary defect. | 7. The optic nerves and retina were normal in both eyes. | 8. External examination was notable for left periorbital swelling, proptosis, and moderate ptosis of the upper eyelid (Figure 1A). | 9. The remainder of the neurologic examination results were normal.An 8-year-old boy presented with 2 weeks of painless proptosis of the left eye (A) accompanied by upper eyelid ptosis and ophthalmoplegia of the left eye (B).

His symptoms began 5 years earlier with right temple numbness, which expanded to include the entire right face and mouth. | 3. He then developed progressive right facial weakness with a droop, slurred speech, and eyelid ptosis. | 4. Finally, binocular vertical and horizontal diplopia and periorbital headaches began. | 5. Trials of gabapentin and steroids provided no relief. | 6. His history was significant for a left cheek melanoma completely excised years prior, numerous cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas of the bilateral head and neck removed without issue, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. | 7. His medications included metformin and simvastatin; he had no history of smoking or drinking. | 8. On examination, he had right-sided ptosis and severe right facial weakness in a lower motor neuron pattern with temporal wasting. | 9. The right pupil was fixed and dilated. | 10. There was no afferent pupillary defect. | 11. The left pupil was appropriately sized and reactive. | 12. His right-sided vision was impaired (20/250) with blurriness. | 13. Vertical and horizontal binocular diplopia was present. | 14. Right extraocular movements were significantly limited in all directions and painful, and right-sided facial sensation was diminished to pinprick in all cranial nerve (CN) V distributions. | 15. His speech was slightly slurred. | 16. Left-sided extraocular movements were intact. | 17. His left facial sensation was intact to pinprick, and his strength was without deficit. | 19. Initial magnetic resonance images (MRIs) were unremarkable. | 20. A biopsy of CN VII was nondiagnostic.

1. A 12-year-old girl with a history of myopia presented to the emergency department complaining of floaters in her right eye for the past 2 weeks. | 2. She had a medical history of patchy hair loss and a violaceous maculopapular rash on the face and upper extremities for 5 years, which was well controlled with topical corticosteroids. | 3. She reported new, sharp headaches in a headband distribution, exacerbated by lights, sounds, and neck flexion. | 4. One week prior to presentation, she experienced a subjective fever and recurrence of the facial rash. | 5. She denied experiencing eye pain, blurry vision, or light sensitivity. | 6. Results of a comprehensive review of systems were otherwise negative. | 7. Family history was notable for antiphospholipid syndrome in her mother. | 8. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OU. | 9. Results of an anterior segment examination, pupil examination, and tonometry were unremarkable. | 10. During dilated ophthalmoscopy, both eyes revealed diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages in the posterior pole and temporal retinal neovascularization, worse in the right eye with associated macular traction and striae. | 11. Both eyes demonstrated extensive peripheral vascular sheathing and retinal capillary nonperfusion (Figure 1). | 12. Fundus photograph composite images of the right eye (A) and left eye (B) demonstrating intraretinal hemorrhages (white arrowheads), superficial retinal hemorrhage (asterisk), and neovascularization (yellow arrowheads) with associated traction and macular striae (black arrowhead) as well as vascular nonperfusion (blue arrowheads) and sheathing (magenta arrowheads).

1. A man in his 60s presented with a 2-month history of painful, occasionally pruritic, fixed erythema on the abdomen. | 2. In addition, the patient suffered from a splenic marginal zone lymphoma with bone marrow infiltration, had a history of splenectomy, and an IgM-κ paraproteinemia. | 3. His hematologic condition was considered stable by his physician, who had also been treating the patient for hepatitis C with ledipasvir-sofosbuvir for 3 months. | 4. On examination, there was a warm erythema on most of the abdomen, which appeared distended owing to hepatitis-induced ascites (Figure, A). | 5. Laboratory results showed an elevated but stable white blood cell count of 19.04 × 103µL (reference range, 3.6-10.5 × 103µL), a recent rise of C-reactive protein levels to 179 mg/L (reference range, 0-5 mg/L), as well as a rise of IgM levels from 1060 mg/dL to 2220 mg/dL (reference range, 34-248 mg/dL) within the past year. | 6. A biopsy procedure was performed on the abdomen (Figure, B-D).A, Light red erythema on most of the abdomen. | 7. B, Interstitial infiltrate of deeply eosinophilic cells in the entire dermis and adjacent subcutis. | 8. Hematoxylin-eosin staining (original magnification ×2). | 9. C, Hematoxylin-eosin staining (original magnification ×40). | 10. D, Original magnification ×10.

1. A woman in her 50s presented to the emergency department with acute, severe, left flank pain. | 2. There was no medical history of trauma, fever, or hematuria. | 3. She was receiving therapy for mantle cell lymphoma and had previously undergone 1 cycle of the Nordic protocol (comprising cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisolone, cytarabine, and rituximab).1  However, this resulted in tumor lysis syndrome and neutropenic sepsis. | 4. The patient was reluctant to undergo further infusional therapy and was switched to ibrutinib, 560 mg, once daily. | 5. During the 2-month period that she was receiving ibrutinib therapy, there were no concurrent administrations of anticoagulants. | 6. At presentation, she was hypotensive (blood pressure, 79/45 mm Hg) with conjunctival pallor and left renal angle tenderness. | 7. The patient’s hemoglobin count was low (7.6 g/dL; reference range, 12-16 g/dL; to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), which represented a significant decrease from the baseline (10.6 g/dL) measured 1 month before presentation. | 8. She was also found to have acute-onset thrombocytopenia (40×109/L; reference range, 140-400×109/L) and leukocytosis (12.75×109/L, reference range, 4-10×109/L). | 9. Her coagulation profile (prothrombin time) was normal.

1. A 4-day-old girl presents with her parents to the pediatrician for a routine visit. | 2. She was feeding well until this morning when she had several episodes of vomiting. | 3. The parents describe the vomitus as “bright green” and the patient has shown little interest in feeding since then. | 4. She was born at 36 weeks gestation to a 37-year-old G2P2 mother. | 5. The patient’s abdominal radiograph can be seen in Figure A and the patient’s upper gastrointestinal series can be seen in Figure B.

1. He was initially treated with topical antibiotics followed by a course of oral sulindac, 200 mg twice daily, without any improvement. | 6. On examination, his visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/25 OS. | 7. Intraocular pressure was 16 mm Hg OD and 23 mm Hg OS. | 8. It was purulent in appearance, but no material was expressed with attempted incision and drainage at the slitlamp. | 10. A culture was positive only for Propionibacterium acnes. | 11. Tests for herpes simplex, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus polymerase chain reactions were negative.External slitlamp photograph showing conjunctival lesion at presentation.

Obtain a lung ventilation-perfusion (V̇/Q̇) scan or pulmonary angiogram.

1. A previously healthy woman in her 50s presented with complaints of increasing forgetfulness, fatigue, and depressed mood after dealing with the deaths of several close relatives. | 2. She was diagnosed with depression and began treatment with antidepressant medication. | 3. After 8 months, she had worsening complaints. | 4. He had a history of hypertension and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which was last treated in 2012 without evidence of recurrence. | 4. His visual acuity was 20/25 OU, and neither fundus was seen to be abnormal. | 5. The vitreous was clear in both eyes. | 6. He denied any recent viral-type illness. | 10. An examination revealed that his visual acuity was still 20/25 OU. | 11. The anterior segment and the anterior vitreous of his right eye were still clear. | 12. However, an examination of the posterior pole of the right eye revealed a light white, deep subretinal/choroidal ring surrounding the optic nerve, with smaller rings around the edge of the larger ring (Figure, A). | 13. The left eye still appeared normal. | 14. The results of fluorescein angiography and fundus autofluorescence were both unremarkable (data not shown). | 16. A, Fundus photograph of the right eye at the time of presentation shows a white-gray ring centered on the optic nerve.

1. A man in his 50s was referred to the dermatology clinic with a diagnosis of granuloma annulare made on the basis of prior skin biopsy results. | 2. He had been treated by a rheumatologist for polyarticular inflammatory arthritis involving the wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, and proximal interphalangeal joints, as well as fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. | 3. Examination revealed numerous, pink-purple dermal papules on the trunk and extremities, with preference for the extensor surfaces of the arms (Figure, A) and legs. | 5. The patient reported a 5- to 7-kg weight loss without fever or sweats. | 6. His pulmonary and joint symptoms were relieved by daily oral prednisone and flared with taper below 10 mg. | 7. Other medications prescribed included hydroxychloroquine, 400 mg, daily for 18 months and weekly adalimumab injections for 7 months, without improvement.A, Pink-purple papules on the extensor surface of the arms. | 8. 1. 1. A 41-year-old woman with a history of ocular hypertension (and using brimonidine tartrate and timolol maleate) was referred by her ophthalmologist for a second opinion regarding yellowish subfoveal precipitates in her left eye. | 2. Of note, he had recently undergone Mohs surgery and subsequent reconstruction for squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the lateral canthus in the fellow eye; he also had a medical history of multiple skin malignant neoplasms. | 5. Slitlamp examination findings were notable for a grayish cornea opacity that appeared to be lusterless, abutting the nasal limbus and extending into the visual axis (Figure 1A). | 6. There was no apparent conjunctival erythema or appreciable feeder vessels at the limbus. | 8. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) indicated that the hyperreflective corneal lesion did not involve the cornea stroma (Figure 1B). | 9. Examination findings at presentation. | 10. A, Slitlamp photograph of the left cornea revealing a translucent gray, lusterless lesion that extends into the visual axis. | 11. B, Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) showing hyperreflective thickened epithelium. | 12. Discuss superficial keratectomy to confirm the diagnosis by histopathologic examination Observation with follow-up for changes over the next 6 to 12 months

She underwent a colonoscopy that showed no intraluminal mucosal abnormalities or masses, but evidence of external compression at the cecum was noted.Coronal (A) and transverse (B) computed tomographic images show a large intra-abdominal cystic mass in the right iliac fossa.

1. A 24-year-old South Asian man presented with acute-onset pain and decreased vision in his left eye. | 2. His ocular history was significant for high myopia, a long-standing traumatic retinal detachment in his right eye, and laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) surgery of the left eye 8 months earlier. | 3. Three months earlier, the patient experienced an episode of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) of the left eye, which was treated with travoprost ophthalmic solution, 0.004%, and oral acetazolamide and resolved. | 4. The patient’s presenting visual acuity was counting fingers OD (baseline) and 20/200 OS. | 5. His initial IOPs were right eye 16 mm Hg and left eye 46 mm Hg by TonoPen. | 6. Examination of the left eye indicated normal gonioscopy results and unremarkable anterior and posterior segment examination findings except for the presence of corneal edema without keratic precipitates. | 7. The patient started treatment with dorzolamide hydrochloride, timolol maleate, brimonidine tartrate, latanoprost, and oral acetazolamide. | 8. The next day, the left eye IOP improved to 28 mm Hg as measured by Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT), with a clear cornea and return of visual acuity to 20/20. | 9. Despite continuing maximum medical therapy for 1 week, the patient’s examination findings remained unchanged. | 10. Because of a concern for possible trabeculitis, he also started treatment with topical prednisolone acetate 4 times daily and oral valacyclovir hydrochloride. | 11. Two days later, the patient returned to the clinic with decreased vision in his left eye, which showed an IOP measured by GAT of 6 mm Hg, visual acuity of 20/400, and a cornea that was edematous (Figure 1). | 12. A, Slitlamp photograph showing a prominent laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) flap in the patient’s left eye. | 13. B, A slit beam focused on the cornea reveals a shallow fluid interface between the stromal bed and the LASIK flap (arrowheads).

His medical history was significant for primary hyperparathyroidism 6 years prior to presentation, for which the patient refused therapeutic management. | 3. The patient was cachectic and exhibited significant muscular weakness. | 4. Clinical examination revealed a large tumor on the distal part of the right fourth finger (Figure, A) that had gradually enlarged in recent months. | 5. Radiography revealed complete lysis of the underlying phalanx and periosteal bone resorption in the phalangeal tuft band.A, The patient initially presented with a large tumor on the distal part of the right fourth finger. | 6. 1. A patient in their 50s presented with asymptomatic keratotic papules, first noticed on the left middle and ring fingers and left toe web spaces more than 10 years earlier. | 2. The papules progressed proximally over the subsequent decade to involve the forearm, arm, scapular area, ankle, shin, and thigh, but only affected the left side of the body. | 3. The patient’s face, palms, soles, and entire right side of the body were spared. | 5. The patient did not have any alopecia, night blindness, or dry eyes or skin. | 6. There was no history of any exposure to radiation or arsenic, nutritional deficiency, inflammatory skin disease, or malignant neoplasm. | 7. There was no family history of a similar condition. | 8. Examination revealed multiple, submillimeter, skin-colored to yellowish keratotic spiny projections over the aforementioned areas, only on the left side of the body (Figure, A and B). | 9. Punch biopsy from a lesion showed orthokeratosis with parakeratotic columns emerging from an epidermal invagination. | 10. The epidermis was mildly acanthotic and with a normal granular layer. | 11. There was a sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. | 12. Adjacent hair follicles were unaffected (Figure, C). | 13. A, Numerous, submillimeter, skin-colored spiny projections over left foot web spaces were present. | 15. C, Histologic results showed a parakeratotic column overlying a mildly acanthotic epidermis with a normal granular layer and keratinocyte maturation. | 16. A sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate was present (hematoxylin-eosin).

1. A 71-year-old man presented to the dermatologist with a 6-week history of a rapidly progressing rash and swelling of the left side of the chest wall. | 2. He had noticed the rash a few days after receiving the second dose of an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna). | 3. He denied itching, weeping, bleeding, or discharge from the rash or the nipple. | 4. He had a history of metabolic syndrome treated with antihypertensives and oral hypoglycemics. | 5. The physical examination showed a morbidly obese White man. | 6. The skin examination showed a 19 × 10-cm pink, fallacious purple color deep-infiltrated papule in the left breast and a similar 15 × 7-cm papule under the left clavicle (Figure, A). | 7. The breast examination was notable for bilateral gynecomastia and inverted left nipple without any palpable lumps. | 8. No lymphadenopathy was noted either. | 9. His laboratory results showed stage 2 chronic kidney disease. | 10. Results of a viral panel including hepatitis A, B, and C and HIV were negative. | 11. The punch biopsy of the skin showed a diffuse island of atypical cells in the dermis (Figure, B). | 12. On immunohistochemical staining, the atypical cells stained positive for CK-7, GATA-3, and PAX-8 (weak focal staining) and negative for estrogen receptor (ER)/progesterone receptor (<1%), TTF-1, SATB-2, CDX-2, and NKX-3.1. | 13. The positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed a diffuse, infiltrating fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid cutaneous lesion on the left chest wall (standardized uptake value, 6.5) and multiple FDG-avid nodes in the axilla (bilaterally), left internal mammary, and left cervical chain.

1. A 23-year-old white man who has sex with men (MSM) presented with a 1-month history of skin lesions on the palms and soles as well as a 2-week history of lesions in his oropharynx. | 2. He reported that a fraction of the lesions had blistered earlier in the course of his illness. | 3. The patient also described myalgias and fatigue over the preceding month. | 4. He moved to Texas from the northeast a few months prior to his illness. | 5. He denied any exposure to sexually transmitted infections or a history of genital lesions. | 6. On examination, the patient had erythematous papules on bilateral palms and soles as well as eroded vesicles on the palate (Figure, A and B). | 7. Lymphadenopathy was not present. | 9. A serologic antibody test revealed an elevated coxsackievirus titer of 1:16 (reference range, <1:8; >1:32 indicative of infection).

1. A 58-year-old woman returned from the Ukraine with 3 months of constant blurry vision in the left eye. | 2. Her history was significant for glaucoma and breast cancer with brain metastasis treated with CyberKnife and whole-brain radiation. | 3. While abroad, she received 2 inferiorly placed periocular steroid injections and was treated with glaucoma drops for elevated pressures of 55 mm Hg. | 4. At presentation, her visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/50 OS, and intraocular pressures were 18 and 20 mm Hg, respectively. | 5. She had a left afferent pupillary defect and left superior visual field deficit. | 6. Slitlamp examination of the right eye was unremarkable, while the left eye showed 1+ cell in the anterior chamber and 1+ nuclear sclerosis with pigment on the anterior lens capsule. | 7. Posterior examination revealed 2+ whitish vitreous deposits, a cup-disc ratio of 0.8, and inferior retinal detachment with subretinal particulate material (Figure, A). | 8. B-scan showed vitreous, subhyaloid, and subretinal opacities without choroidal involvement (Figure, B). | 9. A magnetic resonance image of the brain and orbits did not reveal any new metastatic lesions.A, Whitish vitreous deposits, inferior retinal detachment, and subretinal material seen on fundus photography of the left eye. | 10. B, B-scan ultrasonography of the left eye confirms retinal detachment and hyperechoic subretinal material without choroidal involvement.

1. An otherwise healthy woman in her 30s presented to an outside health care professional with a 2-day history of floaters in her left eye. | 2. She denied additional ocular symptoms and reported no relevant medical, ocular, or family history; medication use; or allergies. | 3. The findings of a review of systems were unremarkable. | 4. A workup for posterior uveitis was initiated, and the patient began therapy with oral antiviral and oral corticosteroid medications. | 5. One week later, her symptoms had worsened, and she was referred for consultation. | 6. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/15 OD and 20/60 OS. | 7. Intraocular pressures, extraocular movements, visual fields by confrontation, and pupil responses were normal. | 8. Anterior segment examination and dilated fundus examination of the right eye had normal findings. | 9. However, the left eye had 3+ anterior chamber cell and 1+ flare, nongranulomatous keratic precipitates, and a clear lens. | 10. The dilated fundus examination revealed 2+ vitritis, a hyperemic disc with blurred margins, macular striae with a blunted foveal reflex, and vascular sheathing with segmental periarteriolar inflammatory plaques in multiple quadrants. | 11. The peripheral retina had well-demarcated peripheral retinal whitening with scalloped margins and intraretinal hemorrhages in all quadrants (Figure 1A and B). | 12. Four days later, repeat fundus photography showed that the peripheral lesions had coalesced into larger circumferential necrotic regions (Figure 1C). | 13. A, Color fundus photography montage of the left eye shows hyperemic disc with blurred margins, vascular sheathing, and peripheral retinal whitening. | 14. B, Magnified image of the temporal retina shows well-demarcated infiltrates with scalloped margins and adjacent intraretinal hemorrhages. | 15. C, Montage from 4 days later shows convergence of necrotic lesions in a circumferential pattern around the equator with confluence in the anterior periphery. | 16. Fresh laser barricade spots are seen at the posterior margin of the areas of necrosis.

A bilateral ocular ultrasonography showed normal results except for vitreous opacity. | 18. Mosaic 9-field 50° fundus photography showed a uniform, glassy, woollike appearance of the vitreous in the right eye (A) and peripheral vitreous opacity in the left after pars plana virectomy (B).

1. A woman in her 70s presented with a new 4-cm left upper lobe lung mass with hilar lymphadenopathy. | 2. Biopsy results demonstrated a squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lung, and chemoradiotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel for stage 3A disease was initiated. | 3. An allergic reaction prompted a change to cisplatin-etoposide, which continued as adjuvant chemotherapy after the radiation was complete. | 4. On examination, he was alert and oriented, with a temperature of 36.3°C, blood pressure of 131/90 mm Hg, heart rate of 94/min, respiratory rate of 18/min with pulse oximetry of 98% on ambient air, and a body mass index of 28.1 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared). | 7. The result of a human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) type 1 antibody test was positive, and CD4 cell count was 73/mm3. | 10. Results of serologic testing for Toxoplasma gondii IgG were negative. | 11. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and spinal MRI were unremarkable.

1. A 58-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a retinal detachment in his left eye. | 2. His visual acuity on presentation was 20/20 in the right eye and hand motion only in the left eye. | 5. A skin punch biopsy demonstrated subtle vacuolar change; rare epidermal dyskeratosis, including within a hair follicle; and superficial perivascular mononuclear cell infiltrate with occasional eosinophils.
